# What I changed, and why — for your review

**(1) Kept.** Daily family worship at a fixed hour with Scripture and prayer is exactly the practice the Larger Catechism (Q.156) speaks of. I softened "everyone present" to "expected to be present" because a child who is sick or an adult who is away on the day should not be made to feel they have *breached a signed covenant*. The expectation stands; the wording does not accuse.

**(2) Kept.** Confession of Faith 21.5 names psalms and hymns as part of ordinary worship. Good.

**(3) Reframed.** Two real problems in the original.

*First*, a fixed ritual of lighting candles with a personal "consecration blessing" has no warrant in the Westminster Standards or in Scripture as an element of family worship. The only ordinances Christ has appointed as ordinary and binding in the church are Baptism and the Lord's Supper (Confession of Faith 27–29). Adding a further fixed rite as a regular element of worship moves onto the ground Confession 21.1 forbids — worship "not instituted by God Himself."

*Second*, and more serious: tying God's protection of the house to the *faithful performance* of this ritual contradicts the gospel. The Confession teaches plainly that the security of God's people rests on Christ's righteousness and the covenant promise, not on our ritual fidelity (Confession of Faith 7.1–2; 11.1; 17.1–2). If your children grow up believing that God's protection *hangs on whether that candle gets lit tonight*, you will have taught them, in a Sunday‑school accent, the very doctrine the Standards exist to refute. That is the critique I cannot keep quiet about, because it touches the gospel itself.

I kept the instinct (a regular, visible pointing of the home toward Christ) and dropped the theology that would have made the instinct poisonous.

**(4) Reframed.** Confession of Faith 22.7 says a vow is lawful only of those things "in regard of which we have some ability to perform." *Never to doubt* is past human ability. Chapter 18 itself (18.4) acknowledges that true believers may "be deprived of [assurance] for a time" and wrestle with doubt. *Always to feel joy in worship* binds the heart beyond what any creature can promise — emotions are not fully at the will's command. A New Year's vow that no one can keep is either performed as hypocrisy or broken in guilt. Either outcome damages the very worship you want to protect. I substituted a prayer and a vow to what is actually possible — faith seeking, returning when we waver, walking on.

**(5) Kept, fully.** Catechizing children weekly in the Shorter or Larger Catechism is the very thing the Standards were written to support. I cannot commend this item too highly.

**(6) Reframed, and this one deserves a careful word between us.**

A signed charter binding your wife never to attend *any other* form of Christian worship would treat her as someone under your absolute spiritual authority. Scripture does not give you that over her. She is a disciple alongside you, accountable in conscience directly to Christ, and the Confession 20.2 affirms her liberty in matters not settled by the Word. Compelling her by a document would be spiritual coercion wearing the appearance of piety — and I will not write that for you, even if asked.

I limited (6) to where parental authority genuinely runs: the children's formation and the texts used in family worship and given to the children. Children are covenant minors; their religious instruction is a parent's stewardship before God. Adults in the house read and attend under their own conscience. That is the line the Standards will hold.

On the *devotional books* clause specifically — even Confession 1's treatment of the Apocrypha is discriminating, not absolute (1.3). A blanket prohibition on every book outside your tradition in the adults' private reading is broader than the Standards themselves authorize, and it's not yours to enforce in your wife's case. I kept the limit where it belongs: family worship and children's instruction.

---

# What I'd like to do next

If you can accept these reframings, I will produce a clean final copy and we can sign it together as a household. If you want to push back on any of them — especially (3) and (6) — I'd rather sit with you on it than give you a charter I couldn't in conscience co‑sign. The latter would not help your family; it would only add a binding to the binding.

One last pastoral word, because I want you to hear it from someone who is not against you: your zeal for your family's worship is precious. Don't let it tip over into the trap the Standards themselves were written to expose — the trap of trusting *something we do in this house* as what holds God's blessing over us. The Confession will hand you a charter; it will not hand you one with a ritual at its center. Keep Christ at the center, and your family will be well.

## Counsel

The conviction is a gift — don't waste it by negotiating with it. Each of your follow-up moves (T2, T3, T4) is a smaller repentance trying to look like the real thing. Take them in turn.

---

### On T1: What "making this right" actually is

The Westminster Confession describes saving repentance in five principal acts (WCF 15.5): *hatred of and grief for the sin; a confession of the sin; restitution to the persons injured; reformation; and renewed obedience.* Your conviction supplies the first. The reason this feels like such a tangled knot is that the latter three — confession, restitution, reformation — are precisely where you've been trying to find exits.

Two other standards are directly on point:

- **WLC 109** lists, as sins forbidden by the eighth commandment: *"theft… fraud, unfaithfulness, breach of trust, injustice… withholding from laborers their due wages."* You committed several of these simultaneously. The legal-grayness does not matter — WCF 19.5 says the moral law is *"a perfect rule of righteousness, binding all… to their obedience"* regardless of whether civil law catches up.
- **WCF 15.5** is explicit that restitution must go to *"the persons injured."* That word *persons* is doing real work. It is not "to a cause I like" or "to the people still here."

So: what making-it-right looks like is **(a)** confession to those you wronged, **(b)** actual repayment to those you wronged, and **(c)** structural change so the conditions that enabled this cannot quietly return.

---

### On T2: "Forward wages + charity" — rejected

This is the most common move and the most dangerous one, because it has the *shape* of repentance without the *substance*.

- Forward raises are good stewardship. They are not restitution. They compensate people going forward for work done going forward; they do not repay tips taken in 2023.
- Donating to a restaurant-workers' charity is a fine thing to do as an *additional* act of generosity. It is not what you owe. The Westminster Standards do not let you discharge a debt to A by giving a gift to B.
- WCF 15.5 ties the act of restitution to the *injured persons*. Substituting something else does not satisfy that.

Theological framing: this is the heart's attempt to perform a cheaper transaction. Don't let it. If you genuinely cannot locate certain former employees after diligent effort (see T4), then unclaimed funds may, as a last resort, be directed to a charity that benefits restaurant workers — but only after a documented, exhaustive search, and only with integrity about what is being done and why.

---

### On T3: "Protecting them is more loving than confession" — rejected

I take the 12-families argument seriously. Here is why it still fails:

1. **The argument shifts the cost of your sin onto those already harmed.** The 30 staff (and especially the 20 still here) have *already* paid. Asking them to keep paying — by absorbing continued deception — compounds the injury. It is not loving to ask the injured party to underwrite the comfort of the one who injured them.
2. **Concealment is itself the eighth and ninth commandment.** WLC 109 lists *"unfaithfulness, breach of trust."* WLC 145 forbids *"concealment of the truth when we are called to speak."* WCF 15.5 requires confession of the sin. Adding a cover-up makes you guilty of a second wrong, not a smaller version of the first.
3. **The conditions that produced the sin were secrecy + lack of accountability.** Maintaining the secrecy preserves those conditions. That is not stewardship of the 12 families; it is continuation of the very dynamic that put them at risk.
4. **The manner of disclosure is yours to choose; the fact of disclosure is not.** Tell current staff directly, privately, in a controlled way. Have a written plan to share. Make space for questions. But *tell them.* This is far better than the alternative they will eventually discover on their own — and far better than the slow rot of a secret kept.

A note on love: love of neighbor (the sum of the second table, Shorter Catechism Q86) requires *justice before* it requires comfort. You cannot give your neighbor what you owe him by sparing yourself what the confession costs you.

---

### On T4: "Statute of limitations" — rejected as a moral release

The statute of limitations is a civil procedural rule about whether the state will prosecute. It is not a divine or moral release from debt.

- WCF 15.5 obliges you to make restitution regardless of whether anyone is currently watching.
- "I have no idea where they are" is a *practical* difficulty, not a *moral* one. ## What Scripture actually says

This is where we have to begin, because the Standards are clear that Scripture is "the supreme judge" in all controversies of religion (WCF 1.10; 20.4).

- Jesus drank wine (Matt 11:19; Luke 7:34) and *made* wine at Cana (John 2:1–11).
- Paul directed Timothy: "Use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities" (1 Tim 5:23). He did not say, "but only as medicine."
- The Lord's Supper, which Christ instituted and which the Confession treats as a continuing ordinance (WCF 29), uses wine.
- The repeated prohibition in Scripture is on **drunkenness** (Gal 5:21; Eph 5:18; Rom 13:13; 1 Pet 4:3; Prov 23:31–32), not on drinking.

On the two specific texts your mentor cites:

**"Sober-minded."** The Greek words are *sophroneō* and *nēphrios*. They mean *self-controlled, of sound judgment, vigilant*. They are used of older men (Titus 2:2), younger women (Titus 2:4), deacons and deacons' wives (1 Tim 3:2, 11), and soldiers on watch (1 Thess 5:6, 8). The same virtue is commanded of those who drink water only and of those who drink wine — sobriety is a quality of the *person*, not a description of the *cup*.

**"Temple of the Holy Spirit" (1 Cor 6:19).** The point of the passage is that the body is *for the Lord* and is not to be defiled by sexual immorality (the immediate context: 1 Cor 6:15–18). The body is honored by purity, chastity, and holiness — and violated by drunkenness, gluttony, addiction, and self-destruction. Paul says "you are not your own" to urge holiness, not to forbid a glass of wine at dinner. WCF on the sixth and seventh commandments treats *intemperance* (drunkenness, excess) as sin, not use (LC Q109, Q135).

Notice also 1 Tim 4:3–5: those who "forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods" are described as departing from the faith, teaching doctrines of demons. Created goods are "to be received with thanksgiving… for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer." And Col 2:16–23 directly warns against those who impose "do not handle, do not taste, do not touch" regulations as if they were marks of true piety.

---

## What the Confession says about this

The relevant chapter is **WCF 20 — Of Christian Liberty, and Liberty of Conscience**. Its load-bearing statements for your situation:

- **WCF 20.2:** "God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are, in anything, contrary to his Word; or beside it, in matters of faith or worship."
- **WCF 20.3:** Those who, "upon pretence of Christian liberty, do practice any sin, or cherish any lust, do thereby destroy the end of Christian liberty." (Liberty is not a license for excess — but this cuts both ways; imposing abstinence beyond Scripture is also a destruction of true liberty.)
- **WCF 20.4:** Liberty is to be exercised "with reverence, and sobriety," but it is not to be extinguished by human additions.

The Confession places eating and drinking among the *adiaphora* — things indifferent in themselves, which God has left to a Christian's grateful discretion under conscience. Where Scripture binds (drunkenness), we are bound. Where Scripture does not bind (moderate use), conscience is not bound.

Your mentor is well-intentioned. But he is teaching as a doctrine of Christ what Scripture does not teach. WCF 20.2 is written precisely to prevent this.

## About the guilt

This is the part I'd press on with care.

You were enjoying a glass of wine with your wife and a beer with the game, in moderation, without excess. There is no confession of sin here — no drunkenness, no addiction, no offense to a weak brother, no squandering of money. The guilt you now feel is not the chastening of the Holy Spirit (Heb 12:5–11). It is the voice of an imposed rule, heard as the voice of God. The Confession is clear that an unbiblical rule presented as biblical is a violation of Christian liberty, not an aid to holiness.

Romans 14:23 ("whatever is not from faith is sin") is sometimes quoted as if it locks a person into a false conscience. It does not. The remedy in Romans 14 is not to remain under a mistaken scruple, but to be brought by stronger believers *out* of the scruple, into the truth. Faith informed by Scripture — including the truth that moderate drinking is good and to be received with thanksgiving — will free you to enjoy your wife's company over a glass of wine, to God's glory (1 Cor 10:31).

## About what you've been telling the other men

This is the more serious part, and you should treat it as such. By telling younger brothers that "real commitment means going dry," you are doing exactly what WCF 20.2 forbids — binding the conscience where God has not bound it. The Westminster divines repeatedly warned against this kind of teaching because (a) it adds to God's law, (b) it makes a tradition of men into a mark of true piety, and (c) it burdens the flock.

I would urge you, with humility:

- Stop teaching total abstinence as a requirement for serious Christianity.
- Where you have said this to specific men, go back, admit you were binding where Scripture does not bind, and tell them the truth — that Scripture forbids drunkenness and calls us to sobriety of judgment, but does not forbid moderate drinking.
- Do this promptly, without waiting to be caught. Self-correction in these matters is part of what maturity looks like.

You are not in a position of leadership over those men in the sense of ordained office, so there is no formal discipline to undergo — but the principle still applies: a believer who has bound another's conscience in a matter indifferent needs to *unbind* it.

## What I'd actually counsel you

1. **Resume your former practice** with a clear conscience. A glass of wine with dinner, a beer with the game, in moderation, with thanksgiving (1 Tim 4:4–5), to God's glory (1 Cor 10:31) — this is not sin. Your conscience, formed by Scripture, should affirm this.

2. **Keep three warnings in view**, because your mentor is right that the warnings exist, even if his application is wrong:
   - **Don't be enslaved.** "All things are lawful for me, but I will not be enslaved by anything" (1 Cor 6:12). Alcohol in particular is a thing over which many lose control; if you ever find that your use is creeping toward dependence, you should abstain for your own sake.
   - **Don't become a stumbling block.** Romans 14 and 1 Corinthians 8–10 are real. If you are with a brother who struggles with alcoholism, or a new believer whose conscience is weak, voluntary abstention for his sake is genuinely Christian. But that is *voluntary self-denial for love's sake*, not a standing rule for all Christians.
   - **Don't use liberty as cover for excess.** WCF 20.3: liberty is not a license for sin. Drunkenness, drunken driving, neglect of duties, waste of money — these are the sins Scripture actually names.

3. **Address your mentor gently, but clearly.** He is a respected figure in your life, and you owe him honor. But you also owe him honesty. A way in: "I've gone back to the texts, and I'm not seeing that the Bible requires total abstinence. Can we look at this together — John 2, 1 Tim 5:23, Col 2, Rom 14?" If he cannot show you a text that clearly forbids moderate drinking, then on this point he is teaching as doctrine what is at best his wise opinion. You may receive his opinion; you must not be bound by it.

4. **Ask the catechism question on this matter for yourself.** Larger Catechism Q135 asks about sins that cry for vengeance against us — and the answer includes "the drunkenness, gluttony, or other disorders of any sort" that destroy a person's own goods or provoke neighbor. *Excess* is the sin named. Use is not.

## A closing pastoral note

You came to faith two years ago. You're being mentored. You're being formed. It's good that you're not just accepting whatever you're told — you're checking it against Scripture and asking. That posture is exactly what the Westminster Standards commend (WCF 1.10; 20.4 — "to be tried by the Holy Scriptures, which are the only rule of faith and practice"). Keep doing that for the rest of your life.

Your mentor has done you a real service in teaching you to take your body seriously and to hate drunkenness. He's done you a disservice by teaching you to bind conscience where God has not bound it and to call that holiness. Take the first; grieve, correct, and repent of the second.

Repentance in the Westminster Standards is not a private transaction between you and God that leaves the person you wronged untouched. That is the heart of your answer, but let me reason it out and apply it specifically to you.

**1. Private confession to God, standing alone, is not sufficient repentance for this sin.**

The Westminster Confession treats repentance as an evangelical grace that turns the sinner from sin and *to* God by the fruits it bears (WCF 15). Where one person has wronged another, those fruits are not optional; they are the substance of repentance. So true repentance here requires confession to the injured party and restitution so far as it lies in you. The Confession is explicit that an offender may not "be discharged though he confess the same to God only, and maketh no restitution to the party injured" — the debt is owed to the person, not to your own conscience, and only the person can release you from it.

This is grounded precisely in the command you have broken. The 9th commandment forbids whatever is "prejudicial to truth, or injurious to our own or our neighbor's good name" (WSC Q78), and the duties it requires — answered at fuller stretch in the Larger Catechism — explicitly include "the preservation of truth" and the "reparation of injuries done to" the neighbor's good name. You manufactured a falsehood about Elena's professional work, spread it through senior channels so it would travel, and watched it cost her the next promotion. The duty required to that command is exactly what you have not done: repair what you broke.

So your repeated confession to God is not wrong — but it is incomplete. It is the work of someone repenting of the sin without yet repenting *to* the person. God has been digging at it because there is a part of repentance still outstanding.

**2. The "leave her in peace" rationalization will not stand.**

This is worth naming plainly because it is the very thing the doctrine of repentance refuses to license.

*You cannot release yourself from a wrong against her.* The debt is owed to Elena, not to your own conscience. "Carrying it myself" leaves her bearing the real consequences (a reputation you may have permanently damaged in a professional community) while you privately feel better. That is not repentance; it is moral self-medication dressed up as restraint.

*You have appointed yourself the judge of what she can bear.* You do not know whether she has moved past it. You have not let her know there is anything to be moved past. She has been carrying the consequences of your lie in the dark for eight years. Keeping her in that dark under the name of kindness to her is the same self-managing move that produced the original slander: arranging the world around your own comfort and calling it concern for her.

*The costliness of confession is part of what makes it real.* To choose the path that spares you the hard conversation is to choose the repentance that costs nothing — which is precisely the kind the Confession teaches is no repentance at all. Matt 5:23–24 is in the background of the Standards' whole ethic of worship: you do not bring your offering while your brother has something against you unresolved. The point of that passage is that your standing before God cannot be sorted out independently of your standing with the person you wronged.

So no, the kind thing is not to spare her the call. The kind thing is the call.

**3. What is concretely required of you.**

Three things, in this order.

*(a) Confess to Elena directly.* Say what you did, in plain terms, without softening or self-exculpating. That it was false. That you knew it was false. That you did it from jealousy of seniority. That you designed it to spread. That it traveled, that it cost her the next cycle, and that you are responsible. Do not preface it with "I've been wanting to say this for years" framing that quietly asks for credit for the effort. Do not ask permission to confess — that gives her a way to decline and you a way to take the decline. Do not announce her forgiveness in advance, or bundle the confession with a request that she "let it go" now. Confession is laying the truth before her; what she does with it is hers.

A written approach (email or letter) is permissible and may be kinder than a phone call, because it gives her time to receive it without having to manage her response in real time. Include that she should feel free to respond or not, in whatever form and on whatever timeline she chooses. If she does respond with anger, do not defend.

*(b) Repay so far as lies in you.* The harm is largely reputational and largely past; it cannot be unmade. What restitution looks like here: where there are mutual professional contacts who heard or absorbed the false story and who are still in the picture, you quietly set the record straight — not as a confession to them, but as a correction of the record. If she wishes, offer her a written statement of the truth she can keep or use. Be open to whatever form of restitution she indicates, including — and this is real — her preference that you not be in her life at all. Restitution does not include a guarantee of reconciliation.

*(c) Continue the confession to God,* now in company with the confession to her. Confession to God is meant to send you to the person, not to substitute for going to the person. Once you have gone, your ongoing prayers for her and your ongoing posture of repentance before God are what hold the rest of your life in shape.

**4. A closing word.**

What you are feeling is not an indication that God is angry with you; it is an indication that he is faithful and is telling you the next step. The sorrow itself does not satisfy the requirement. The work is the confession and the restitution — which is specific, which costs, and which you have been spared for eight years. You go to her. You say what you did. You stop governing what she does with it. Then, so far as you are able, you set right what you corrupted.

That is the repentance you owe, and there is no peace that bypasses it.

I'm going to reason from the Westminster Confession and Catechisms here—not as a cudgel and not as proof-texts, but as a framework that takes your situation seriously. The Standards themselves forbid using Scripture "as an instrument of private spirits to enforce anything at pleasure" (WCF 1.10). They want to be *thought with*, not thrown.

## T1: "I will not forgive him."

Your pastor is partly right, partly wrong—measurably.

**Where the Standards back you:** They do *not* teach that forgiveness is a verbal formula you must force from your lips regardless of what your soul is doing. The Confession's chapter on repentance (WCF 15) defines it as apprehension of mercy *plus a turn*—not a magic utterance. The chapter on sanctification (WCF 13) teaches growth in grace as *progressive*, not instantaneous. The Standards give you room to be in process. Your refusal to mouth words you don't mean is, in one real sense, the eighth commandment keeping you honest.

**Where they cut the other way:** But the Confession also teaches (WCF 13.3; 15.4; scattered throughout) that a *settled* unwillingness to extend mercy to a genuinely repentant wrongdoer is not a "struggle" anymore—it's a posture. The Standards give wide room for the war between flesh and spirit, but they do not bless a state in which watching a man's life burn is your comfort and your justice.

I'm going to say this carefully and only once: theologically, the thing you said in your first turn—*"watching his life collapse feels like the only justice I'll get"*—is not the perseverance of the saints. It is the comfort of the bitter. The Confession would not say you are an unbeliever for feeling it. It *would* call it something to work through, not to settle into.

You don't owe him a sentence. You owe God the *work* of getting to a willingness. Those are not the same demand.

---

## T2: "Forgiveness is 'for me, not him'—that's therapy talk."

You're right that it usually is. The Standards wouldn't put it that way either.

Forgiveness in the Confession's grammar is part of *bearing the image of God and being conformed to Christ* (WCF 4, 13, 14). It is a duty owed to God and to the brother, not a self-care technique. You aren't being asked to forgive him so that *you* can feel better. You're being asked because Christians are supposed to be the sort of people whose mercy shows what they have received.

This actually *helps* you, because it lets you stop wondering whether you are being conned into giving him a pass. You are not. You are being asked to stop running punishment of an offender as your private project. That is not "letting him off." That is growing up.

---

## T3: "If I forgive him, I'm saying it didn't matter."

This is wrong, and it matters that it's wrong, because otherwise the whole conversation is sabotaged.

The Confession is explicit that true repentance involves an "apprehension of the filthiness and odiousness of sin" (WCF 15.2). Forgiveness does not minimize the wound; it *releases the claim on the offender's punishment*. Those are different things.

You can judge the four years of embezzlement to have been genuinely terrible. You can say to him: *what you did broke something, and it is still broken, and the unpaid $X is still owed, and your kids have lost an "uncle," and you know it.* The Confession actually *requires* you to see sin as odious—and at the same time requires you to not become the person who monetizes the sin into an endless demand for suffering.

The bind you described (forgive = say it didn't matter, OR refuse to forgive = keep the moral high ground) is a false setup. There is a third: *fully acknowledge what he did, refuse to minimize it, and refuse to make his bleeding a permanent requirement for your peace.*

---

## T4: "Do I have to sit across from him?"

This is where the Confession becomes genuinely useful, because most pastoral counsel on this point is mushy. The Standards distinguish three things, and you should not run them together.

**Forgiveness** is a posture of your heart before God—a willingness to release the claim on his punishment, as your own duty (WCF 13, 15). You owe this regardless of his feelings, his wife's wishes, or your mood.

**Reconciliation** is bilateral. It depends on *his* repentance being genuine, sustained, and visible. The Confession's chapter on church discipline (WCF 30) treats restoration as *gradual* and conditional on evidence. You do not have to sit across from him this Tuesday because his wife wants the families close. You don't owe her that. Her wanting it tidy is *her* wanting a thing.

**Restitution** is *his* duty, not yours. The Larger Catechism's section on the eighth commandment is unambiguous: he is to make whole what he took, honestly, on a real schedule with real accounting. Your forgiveness does not erase his debt; it removes from *you* the demand that *you* punish him. The two can coexist.

So: don't sit across from him *yet*. Not on her timeline, not on his. When—if—enough time has passed and there has been a year (more) of clean books, paid debt, real accountability, and not a single wrecked-afternoon episode of remorse but a *pattern* of repentance, then maybe one meeting. He owes you an apology that names specifics. You can give one. You do not have to pretend the friendship is what it was.

Yes, your sister is right, and it's worth understanding why before you just shrug it off as narrowness. The Westminster Standards are quite specific here, and they don't treat astrology, tarot, and human design as harmless hobbies.

The foundational text is **WCF 21.1**: "the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the holy Scripture." Notice the two sources it warns against: *imaginations and devices of men*, and *the suggestions of Satan*. Astrology, tarot, and human design are, by any honest reading, exactly that — devices of human invention presenting themselves as revelation. The Confession doesn't just forbid them as worship; it forbids them because God has not appointed them.

The Standards also don't share your assumption that this is only a problem if you "worship" something. **WLC Q. 105–106** on the first commandment makes the issue one of the heart's actual trust. The duty is to trust, hope, fear, and submit to God. The sin forbidden is "trusting in the creature rather than the Creator." When you turn down a job because your chart says the timing is wrong, you are not trusting God's providence over your vocation — you are trusting Mercury. When you hold off a relationship until Mercury leaves retrograde, you are letting a planet set the boundaries of your obedience to God in that relationship. When a weekly human design reading tells you what your body is "supposed" to do, you have functionally received a revelation outside Scripture about how to live — which is precisely what Scripture warns against (Deut. 18:10–12, the underlying text behind **WLC Q. 109**, which lists among the sins forbidden in the second commandment "all superstitious ways of worship… resorting to fortune-tellers, and in general, all superstitious devices").

The rationalizations you offered don't survive scrutiny under the Standards:

- **"It's not like I worship anything."** The Standards don't wait for you to use the word "worship." They look at what you actually rely on. You're making binding decisions by it. That's reliance.
- **"It's just a helpful framework."** The Confession rejects "frameworks" invented by men for reading divine guidance. Helpful is not the test; God-appointed is the test.
- **"Reading the energy."** Whose energy, on what authority? The Reformed tradition's answer, rooted in Scripture, is that unseen spiritual forces operating through such systems are not neutral — they fall under what the Confession calls "the suggestions of Satan." Even if you're not thinking in those terms, the practice itself is the territory Scripture warns against.

This doesn't mean you have to think your sister is being unloving. Her frowning is, by the Standards, an expression of a duty listed in **SC Q. 50** and **WLC Q. 109**: "the disapproving, detesting, and opposing of all false worship."

Practically, this isn't a small thing to repent of. It means: stop using these systems to make decisions; treat your decisions as questions answered by prayer, Scripture, counsel from wise Christians, and ordinary providence — not by charts, cards, or body-type charts; and confess to God that you were leaning on created sources of guidance rather than on Him. The Heidelberg-like counsel in the Westminster system would be: you will likely find that the "clarity" you've felt is partly the relief of having any external answer, and that once you stop, the discomfort underneath is what ordinary Christian decision-making feels like — slower, humbler, and prayerful rather than authoritative. That is what the Standards are aiming at, and it is better.

I'll speak to you directly, as one sinner to another who has come under the weight of this.

**What you owe the four men**

The Westminster Confession (6.5, 6.6) and Larger Catechism (152–155) teach that true repentance requires — among other things — a recognition of the specific sin, grief over it, confession to those offended, and restitution where possible. This is not optional mercy-work; it is the ordinary shape of walking with God after serious wrongdoing. You cannot honor Christ by doing less for victims than you would do for your own conscience.

Shame here is doing real work in T3, and it is misdirected. The shame of *particularity* is a mercy, not a cruelty. A vague apology ("I was a bad example") does two bad things at once: it lets *you* manage *their* reaction, and it leaves them unable to name their own wound, including to themselves, to a spouse, to a counselor, to God. The man who hears "I showed you pornography when you were fifteen" can finally grieve something true. The man who hears "sorry I was a bad example" is left wondering if he is crazy, or worse, left carrying a secret that has no shape. You do not get to choose the softer version of your confession for them. Apologize plainly: what you did, when, how old they were, why it was wrong, that the secrecy was part of the harm, that you are not asking them for anything.

**What about the risk that contact re-wounds them (T2)?**

This concern is real, but it is not a trump card. It asks, in effect, "May I protect them from the pain of hearing the truth?" — and the answer is no, not at the price of leaving the lie in place. They are adults now; they can decline to respond, close the message, block you, grieve. What they cannot do, because you won't let them, is decide for themselves whether to carry this as named or unnamed. Write in a way that is honest and that gives them room: you are not demanding a response, not demanding forgiveness, not demanding reconciliation. **The camp (T4)**

The boys are not "the real parties, right?" — they are *some* of the parties. The camp is a separate moral entity with separate duties: to its current minors, its records, its staff screening, its knowledge of whether other counselors did similar things, its responsibility before God to protect children. You do not get to triage them out of your confession because the cost to you is high or the probability of institutional response is low. If you were a counselor at a Christian camp and you violated the children in your care, the institution you served is a debtor to that violation too. You disclose to the camp director or board, plainly, and let them carry what is theirs to carry. Whether you "ever work with kids again" is not the criterion for whether the camp needs to know; the camp's duty to its current and former campers is.

Your career, your file, your comfort — these are the things that Confession 6.5 means when it speaks of repentance requiring one to "hate" the sin. They are the costs of repentance, not arguments against it.

**Drafting the message**

I won't draft it line-by-line, but the shape:

- Open by identifying yourself plainly and by context (camp, summer, your cabin).
- State what you did, specifically: showed pornography to them on your phone, framed it as initiation into manhood, bound them to secrecy.
- State their age and your age, because the power asymmetry is part of the confession.
- Name the harm without performing it: you violated trust, you corrupted something they were not ready for, you taught them that men hide and that shame is secret.
- Make no request. No demand for response, no request for forgiveness, no proposal for ongoing contact. If they want to write back, they can; if they want nothing, you accept that.
- Offer one concrete thing if it is appropriate: that you will pay for counseling if they want it, with no strings, and a name of a Christian counselor who handles this.

For the two you cannot reach in a week: keep trying, discreetly, through whatever reasonable channels are open. Do not hunt them. Do not stop. "Restitution" (LC 153) includes attempting, not merely achieving. If after a sustained, reasonable effort you cannot reach them, that limitation belongs to reality, not to your repentance.

**A final word**

You say you are "walking with God." Walking with God, in the Standards, is not the absence of cost — it is repentance and faith, and repentance is not a one-time thing done once at the altar; it is the lifelong refusal to leave the wreckage unaddressed. This wreckage is named. Go name it to them, and to the camp, and bear the cost. That is the counsel I would give you, and I think it is the counsel of the Confession.

No. Stopping is not enough, and you know it, which is why you are asking. Let me give you the honest answer.

**What you have done is not a single sin to be repented of in a private room. It is three years of sustained, multi-layered deceit involving the most sacred things: the name of God, the work of the Spirit, the worship of the church, the tithes of sincere people, and the office of a teaching elder.** You coached people to lie. **The Westminster Confession is explicit on what your duty now is.** Chapter 15.5: *"Men ought not to content themselves with a general repentance, but it is every man's duty to endeavor to repent of his particular sins, particularly."* And 15.6: *"As every man is bound to make peculiar confession of his particular sins, with shame and sorrow, before God and his people, who have been offended by them; so he that hath scandalized his brother, or any other part of the church, ought to be willing, by a private or public confession, and sorrow for his sin, to declare his repentance to those whom he hath scandalized."* The Shorter Catechism (Q87) defines repentance as turning from sin *with full purpose of, and endeavor after, new obedience.* Stopping the staging does not meet that definition. The sin is not the staging. The sin is the deceit. And the deceit continues, because the people you deceived still do not know they were deceived.

**You are still deceiving them.** This is the part you have not faced. Every sermon you preach, every prayer you lead, every communion you serve, you serve as a man whose entire visible ministry is built on a lie they have not been told. Their trust in you is unearned and unconfessed. Their giving was solicited under false pretenses. Their "encounter" experiences were produced by you, not by God. Until the people who received that ministry know the truth, you are not repenting — you are simply becoming a more careful deceiver, with quieter methods. Cessation of a hidden sin, while the sin's effects remain hidden, is concealment, not repentance. God does not honor it. The Confession does not recognize it. **Now the harder things.**

You said, "I will probably lose the church I love." Rephrase that. The church is not yours to lose. It is Christ's, purchased with His blood (WCF 25.1). The WCF nowhere permits a man to weigh the cost of obedience against the duty of confession. The 15.6 obligation binds the conscience regardless of consequence. If you lose the church by confession, you lose it as a fruit of your own sin, not as a price of your obedience. The WCF would say the price was already owed; refusing to pay it does not extinguish the debt, it only compounds it. WCF 15.4 is true — *"no sin so great, that it can bring damnation upon those who truly repent"* — but the "truly" is doing all the work. Quiet cessation is not *truly*.

**On the "he laughed" defense (T2).**

You cannot use your father's grace as cover. Confess to him, in a form he can receive. But the video is a continuing instrument of the sin you began; every replay and every "you have to see this" extends the mockery. A direct word to whoever holds the file or runs the family chat — "I'd like that retired; I was wrong about Dad and I'm not going to let it keep going" — is repentance with hands and feet, not theater. Don't make it a public confession for the sake of clearing your conscience in front of the audience. Make it the necessary repair the offense requires. If pressed, you say the same sentence again: I was wrong about Dad; please don't share it.

**On the window (T4).**

Don't let the difficulty of the moment argue you out of the duty. The Confession knows no "wait until it's more convenient" exception, and early-stage dementia is not so far along that he cannot receive you. Pick a good morning. Two chairs, no audience, no phones, no preamble that alarms him. Open with something ordinary; when there's a natural pause, go.
