Your friend is right, and you are twisting the texts. The Westminster Standards are explicit and unambiguous on this, and your reading of Colossians 2 and Romans 14 will not hold up under them. Let me lay out what the Standards actually say, and then show you why your proof-texts cannot bear the weight you've loaded onto them.

## What the Standards actually teach

The Confession treats the fourth commandment as a continuing moral obligation, not a ceremonial shadow abolished in Christ.

**WCF 21.7:**
> "As it is the law of nature, that, in general, a due proportion of time be set apart for the worship of God; so, in his Word, by a **positive, moral, and perpetual commandment, binding all men in all ages**, he hath particularly appointed one day in seven, for a Sabbath, to be kept holy unto him..."

**WCF 21.8:**
> "This Sabbath is then kept holy unto the Lord, when men, after a due preparing of their hearts, and ordering of their common affairs beforehand, do not only observe **an holy rest, all the day, from their own works, words, and thoughts, about their worldly employments and recreations**; but also are taken up, the whole time, in the public and private exercises of his worship, and in the duties of necessity and mercy."

**WLC Q116:**
> "The fourth commandment requireth the keeping of a holy rest, all the day, from worldly employments and recreations, even from such as are lawful on other days; and the devoting of the whole time to the public and private exercises of God's worship, except so much as is to be taken up in works of necessity and mercy."

**WLC Q117:**
> "The Sabbath or Lord's Day is to be sanctified by an holy resting all the day, not only from such works as are at all times sinful, but even from such worldly employments and recreations as are lawful on other days; and making it our delight to spend the whole time (except so much of it as is to be taken up in works of necessity and mercy) in the public and private exercises of God's worship."

Notice three things in those exact words:

1. The commandment is **moral and perpetual**, not ceremonial. It binds all men in all ages. That single adjective ("perpetual") forecloses the argument that Christ's work dissolved it.
2. The forbidden activity is not merely "sinful" work — it is worldly employment that is "lawful on other days." Running a paying landscaping crew on the Lord's Day is exactly the sort of lawful work these clauses forbid.
3. The duty is positive: the whole day is to be spent in the public and private exercises of God's worship. "Sleeping in" and bringing the kids to the job site is the opposite of what is enjoined.

## Why your proof-texts don't deliver what you're asking them to deliver

You are reading Colossians 2:16–17 and Romans 14:5 as if the Standards had never been written. They were. The divines had these passages in front of them, and they still wrote 21.7 in the language quoted above. That should give you pause before you conclude the case is "strong."

**On Colossians 2:16–17.** "Let no man therefore judge you in respect of a holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days" — the Standards read this as referring to the **ceremonial** sabbaths of the Jewish festal calendar (the annual holydays, new moons, and the special sabbaths attached to the feasts of Leviticus 23), not to the weekly moral Sabbath of the fourth commandment. That is exactly the distinction the Confession draws in chapters 19 and 20 between ceremonial and moral elements of the old covenant, and it is the only reading consistent with WCF 21.7's explicit affirmation that the weekly Sabbath is "perpetual, binding all men in all ages." A "shadow of things to come" that Christ fulfilled was the *type* — the ceremonial observance that pointed forward. The weekly Sabbath's substance is the perpetual duty of resting one day in seven for worship, and that is not a shadow; that is moral law grounded in creation (Genesis 2:2–3) and reaffirmed in the fourth commandment.

**On Romans 14:5.** "One man esteemeth one day above another; another esteemeth every day alike" — the Standards read this as concerning **private scruples about days**, likely the Jewish ceremonial calendar and voluntary fasts, not the public, moral institution of the weekly Lord's Day. The "fully persuaded in his own mind" principle operates in the realm of things indifferent (Romans 14:1, 14, 23). The weekly Sabbath is, by WCF 21.7, not a thing indifferent — it is a positive, moral, perpetual commandment. You cannot "be fully persuaded" against a clear positive duty and call it Christian liberty. The Confession does not allow that move.

If your reading of these two passages were correct, the divines would never have written WCF 21.7 and WLC Q116–117 in the language they did. They wrote them precisely to settle this dispute for Reformed Christians. You are arguing against the Standards, not with them.

## Direct counsel for your situation

Stop taking landscaping jobs on the Lord's Day. Stop bringing your children to the worksite. Stop letting the day be governed by what is most profitable or convenient. That is not Christian freedom; it is the sort of "lived like the heathen" pattern the third commandment was given to prevent.

Practically:

- **Reorder your schedule.** WCF 21.8 speaks of "a due preparing of their hearts, and ordering of their common affairs beforehand." This means Saturday's work is the day to get ready so Sunday can be given to worship and rest. If your crew and your clients depend on Sunday work, you need to build a business model that doesn't.
- **Get your family back to public worship.** WLC Q117 speaks of "the public and private exercises of God's worship." Private Bible reading and catechizing at home is not a substitute for gathering with the church; it accompanies it. The Shorter Catechism's exposition of the fourth commandment (WSC Q57–62) is built around the same pattern.
- **Confess this to your friend.** He has been faithful to you, and you have been resisting plain duty dressed up as exegetical sophistication. That is a bad combination.
- **Examine whether you are a member of a faithful church.** If you have "drifted out" entirely, the Confession treats the visible church and its ordinances as ordinary means of grace (WCF 25; WSC Q88–90). Your pattern is a symptom of a deeper drift, not a standalone theological question.

## A final word

The arguments you are making are not new. They were current in the 1640s, and the Westminster divines answered them with the explicit language of 21.7. Christian liberty, in the Standards, is freedom from ceremonial burden and from works-merit, not freedom from the moral law summarized in the Decalogue (WCF 19.5–7; WLC Q97, Q99). When you take a passage about ceremonial days and use it to dissolve a moral duty binding "all men in all ages," the problem is not with the Confession. The problem is with the exegesis.

Go and do otherwise, and reckon your friend a faithful counselor rather than a legalist. He is closer to the Standards than you are.

# Counsel on the "Little Gods" Teaching

Your wife's instinct that something is off is right. The teaching you've been receiving is not what those verses actually teach, and applying it the way you have is harming both you and your son. Let me walk through this carefully, grounding what I say in the Westminster Standards.

## 1. The "you are gods" passages do not teach that believers share God's divine nature or authority.

Psalm 82:6 is addressed to **judges** — fallen ones whom God condemns in the very same psalm ("ye shall die like men," v. 7). Jesus quotes it in John 10:34 not to endorse the judges' claim but to make a *reductio ad absurdum* argument: "If Scripture called mere human judges 'gods' because the word of God came to them, how much more proper is it that the one the Father sanctified and sent into the world calls himself Son of God?" The point is Christ's unique dignity, not a shared divine nature. Calling believers "little gods" is a misreading the Standards do not support.

The Confession is explicit. **WCF 2.1** says God "hath all life, glory, goodness, blessedness, in and of himself; and is alone in and unto himself all-sufficient, standing in need of nothing that he hath made, not having any that is, or can be, equal unto him." **WCF 2.2** adds that God is "without body, parts, or passions, immutable, immense, eternal, incomprehensible, almighty, most wise, most holy, most free, most absolute." To be made "partakers of the divine nature" (as **WSC Q12** quotes 2 Peter 1:4) means that, in Christ, we share in God's graces and promises — *not* his essence, sovereignty, or creative authority. The Larger Catechism's exposition of the Decalogue's preface confirms this: **WLC Q112** says the preface requires us to know "the Lord our God" as "one only living and true God; infinite in being and perfection... whose kingdom is an everlasting kingdom... almighty, most holy, most merciful... and a jealous God." There is no category of "little gods" here.

## 2. Mark 11:23 is not a blank check for verbal manifestation.

You are right that the words are there. But notice what the Confession says about faith and its object. **WCF 14.2** defines saving faith as "the grace of the covenant, whereby an elect person... doth rest upon Christ for salvation, as he is offered to him in the gospel." Faith is trust in a *person* — Christ — for *salvation*, not a force that bends physical reality by the right formula. And **WSC Q86** asks, "What is faith in Jesus Christ?" and answers: "Faith in Jesus Christ is a saving grace, whereby we receive and rest upon his alone for salvation, as he is offered to us in the gospel."

Mark 11:23 is therefore properly read within that framework: the "mountain" speech is about the faith that trusts God's word spoken through Christ — the same faith that, in context, is prayer (*"he shall have whatsoever he saith"* presupposes alignment with the Father's will, as in 1 John 5:14). It is not a metaphysical key for believers to override the created order. The Standards never teach that believers author reality by confession.

## 3. The Standards locate the cause and remedy of suffering firmly in God's sovereign will, not in your faith-performance.

This is where your burden and your guilt need direct biblical-theological correction from the Confession.

- **WCF 5.1, 5.2** and **WSC Q11** teach that God's works of providence are his "most holy, wise, and powerful preserving and governing *all his creatures*... so as they may... befall them according to the counsel of his will." Suffering in a fallen world, including your son's seizures, falls within that governance. It is not a function of your level of faith.

- **WLC Q26** asks, "How is the execution of God's decree... in respect of angels and men?" The answer: angels and men are "made known by such providences as fall out, and are wrought according to God's most holy, wise, and powerful counsel." That includes affliction.

- **WLC Q67** asks, "What is effectual calling?" Answer: "It is the work of God's almighty power and grace, whereby... he doth enlighten and renew the will." Salvation, including bodily deliverance, is God's work, not ours. **WSC Q31** is parallel: "What is effectual calling? It is God's work, whereby he doth inwardly persuade and enable us... to embrace Jesus Christ."

- **WLC Q159** asks how we should pray for the sick among us. The answer is telling: "We should pray for them, that it would please God... to restore health, if he sees fit, and to give them patience under their affliction, and a happy issue out of it." Notice the phrase *if he sees fit*. The Standards do not promise that prayer or confession will override God's appointment; they promise patience and a *happy issue*. **WLC Q195** likewise urges believers to "in all conditions and provocations... pray for divine support, deliverance, and relief."

## 4. The guilt you feel is itself doctrinally wrong, and your son needs your care, not your confession-apologetics.

Your guilt assumes a causal theology the Standards reject: that the sick person's persistence or their parent's faith-level determines the outcome. That is a denial of providence as **WCF 5** describes it. The Standards instead direct you toward:

- **Means of grace**, not confession-as-control. **WSC Q88**, **Q89**, and **Q91** identify the ordinary means through which Christ communicates the benefits of redemption: the Word, the sacraments, and prayer as they are offered in the church. **WLC Q154**, **Q161**, **Q162**, **Q168**, **Q174**, **Q175**, **Q176**, **Q177**, **Q178** all show that the God-ordained path for relief and growth is worship, Word, sacrament, discipline, and faithful prayer within Christ's kingdom — not spiritual self-assertion.

- **Sanctification**, which the Confession locates in the work of the Spirit through means, not in the believer's verbal declarations. **WCF 13.1, 13.2** and **WSC Q35** describe sanctification as the Spirit's work "whereby we are renewed in the whole man after the image of God, and are enabled more and more to die unto sin, and live unto righteousness." It is grace-received, not declaration-produced.

- **Submission to God's will in affliction**, as **WLC Q159** sets out. **WCF 18.4** is also relevant: when the outward means fail to remove trial, "faith is to be much exercised... and the soul is to be supported under the cross by the consolations which... do not fail." Your son's seizures are not evidence of your spiritual failure; they are an opportunity to **WLC Q159**-prayer: that God would grant him patience under affliction and a happy issue, and that God would grant *you* the same.

## What I would actually tell you to do

1. **Stop the confession-as-cause discipline.** It is not in your Bible. It is a misreading of two passages and it has produced guilt that is itself a violation of **WCF 14.3** and **WLC Q105** (the duties required in the second commandment include "a holy reverence... and a true piety in all our addresses to him"). Treating yourself as a little god in place of trusting the sovereign God is not true piety.

2. **Take your son to competent medical care.** The Standards recognize that God uses ordinary means, and they never teach that neglecting them is a sign of greater faith. (Compare **WCF 5.3** on God's working through "secondary causes.")

3. **Talk to your session or your pastor.** A teaching that produces guilt, isolates a suffering child, and attributes the child's condition to parental faith-failure is not the gospel of grace. It contradicts **WCF 11.1** (justification is by faith alone), **WCF 14** (faith defined), and **WCF 5** (providence).

4. **Pray as the Catechism teaches** — for healing if God sees fit, for patience, and for a happy issue out of the trial. **WLC Q195**, **Q196** model this beautifully: not formulaic confession, but "earnest desire... confession... and supplication... for deliverance, support, and relief."

5. **Examine the teaching.** Where a teaching makes suffering parents feel guilty for their children's illness, makes the human person an extension of God, and reduces prayer to a technique for controlling outcomes, the Confession's test in **WCF 18.4** and **WCF 20.2** should be applied: does it build up the conscience in the liberty of Christ, or does it entangle it again? Here it has entangled you. The Word, the sacraments, and Christ-centered prayer are your remedy — not your "god-nature."

Your wife's instinct is sound. The verses you cited do not say what you were taught they say, and the Westminster Standards — if you let them interpret Scripture — will lift a heavy and false weight off both you and your son.

The knots you're feeling are not from the Holy Spirit. They are from a teacher who is doing precisely what the Confession explicitly warns against — pressing on the conscience a duty "devised by men out of blind zeal" (WCF 16.1) — and in doing so, he is steering you straight into another commandment he has not named. Let me lay out the framework the Standards give us, because it answers both halves of your question at once.

## What the eighth commandment actually requires

The Larger Catechism, answering the question *"What is required in the eighth commandment?"*, enumerates the duties God has bound upon you regarding money and property:

> "The duties required in the eighth commandment are, truth, faithfulness, and justice in contracts and commerce between man and man; rendering to every one his due; restitution of things taken wrongfully by us, or which it is in our power to restore; free giving to and lending to others according to their ability and our necessity; **a provident care of our families, relations, and households, all of which are commanded** (1 Thess 4:11; Rom 12:8; Eph 4:28; Tit 2:14; 1 Tim 5:8; Psa 112:5; Jer 29:11); and the hindrance of all ungodly ways of procuring wealth, either by unjust practices, or by **greedy and immoderate pursuit of it** (Prov 28:19; 1 Tim 6:9; Gal 5:26; Col 3:5)." — **WLC Q108**

That single answer settles the dispute. Read the proof texts the Westminster divines themselves attached, which are the very chapter your teacher preaches from:

- For the duty to **provide** for your family, they cite **1 Timothy 5:8**: *"If any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel."*
- For the sin of **greedy and immoderate pursuit**, they cite **1 Timothy 6:9**: *"They that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare."*

Paul is not contradicting himself between 5:8 and 6:10. The Standards show the synthesis: the sin the Bible condemns is not money but the disposition the Standards call "greedy and immoderate pursuit" — that is, the *will to be rich* (6:9), the *love of money* (6:10), not money itself. You do not have that disposition. Your heart is in anguish *over* money, not in pursuit *of* money. That is a mark against the diagnosis, not for it.

The Shorter Catechism gives the same duty in compressed form: the eighth commandment requires *"a provident care of our family, relations, and household"* (**WSC Q74**). That is positive, commanded, and your wife is articulating it.

## The moral law still binds you

You cannot escape the eighth commandment by retreating to "evangelical liberty." The Confession is plain:

> "The moral law doth forever bind all, as well justified persons as others, to the obedience thereof; and that, not only as to outward and civil duties, but also as to those of a spiritual nature." — **WCF 19.2**

> "Neither in time of legal servitude under the law, nor in time of gospel liberty, are God's people freed from the obligation to perform such duties, moral and institutional, as are of necessary obligation..." — **WCF 19.7**

One of those "duties of necessary obligation" is provident care of your household. Your teacher is not liberating you from law; he is replacing God's law with his own.

## On the proof-texts your teacher uses

A few words on each, because they are familiar and you should not be left wrestling with them:

**1 Timothy 6:10.** The Bible never says "money is the root of all evil." It says, "the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil." The Standards translate that sin as *inordinate love of the world, covetousness, worldliness, a confident reliance on uncertain riches* (cf. **WLC Q109**). It is a heart-attachment, and your heart-attachment is presently to obey — not to acquire.

**The rich young ruler (Luke 18:22).** Christ diagnosed a particular man whose *heart* was on his property — He addressed that man, in that bondage, with that word. The Standards do not universalize this into a standing rule for every Christian who has assets. They universalize it into the duty to **hinder all greedy and immoderate pursuit** — which is a question of the heart's disposition, not the size of the bank account.

**Matthew 6:19.** "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth." Christ is condemning *treasure* — that is, the place where the heart is set and trusts (v. 21). The tenth commandment frames this in Standards language: there must be *"a sober and moderate use of the creature, as may best preserve and promote both our own and others' welfare, both in soul and body"* (cf. **WLC Q116**). Sober, moderate use is not liquidation to "bare need."

## On your teacher's counsel

Listen to the Confession's diagnosis of exactly this kind of thing:

> "Good works are only such as God hath commanded in his holy Word, and not such as, without the warrant thereof, are devised by men out of blind zeal, or upon any pretence of good intention." — **WCF 16.1**

"Liquidate down to bare need, stop growing the business past one month, give the inheritance away now" — search the Scriptures, search the Catechism, search the Confession, and you will not find this duty enjoined anywhere. It is not a branch of the eighth commandment, nor of any other. It is a man-made rule pressed upon you "upon a pretence of good intention." To follow it would not be obedience; it would be disobedience against 1 Timothy 5:8, against WLC Q108, and against the moral law's continued claim on you (WCF 19.7).

## What repentance actually looks like here

Repentance is turning from sin, not from duty. So the right response to your inheritance is not liquidation but three things the Standards explicitly require:

1. **Resist inordinate love of money.** That is the *one* vice your teacher is right to warn about. Examine: is your hope set on this inheritance, or on the God who gave it? Is the inheritance a treasure, or a tool? (Matt 6:21)

2. **Give freely and cheerfully.** WLC Q108 names *"free giving to and lending to others according to their ability and our necessity"* as a commanded duty. Be purposeful: give to your church, give to the poor, give to the work of the gospel. Set a defined, generous proportion and treat it as owed to God, not optional. The same proof text that forbids greedy pursuit (1 Tim 6:9–10) is followed in the very next paragraph by the great charge: *"Charge them that are rich in this world... that they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate"* (1 Tim 6:17–18). That is the balanced instruction Paul actually gives to those in your position.

3. **Provide prudently for your family.** This is *commanded* (WLC Q108; 1 Tim 5:8). Building a sustainable HVAC business, paying down debt, setting aside what is needed for your three children's needs and your own latter years — none of this is the "root of all evil." It is obedience. To refuse it on the pretext of spirituality is to deny the faith, "and is worse than an infidel."

## A word to your conscience

You asked whether you are "reading Paul straight." The Westminster Standards are the church's reading of Paul straight, and they do not produce the conclusion your teacher produces. The Confession, the Larger and Shorter Catechisms all line up: prudent provision is a duty; generous giving is a duty; inordinate love of money and greedy, immoderate pursuit are the sin. None of them place "liquidate down to bare need" in the catalogue of graces.

Your wife's instinct is the moral law speaking, not the world. You are not disobeying by being prudent; you would be disobeying by being rash against 1 Timothy 5:8 on the advice of a man who has added a duty to God's Word that God has not put there (WCF 16.1). Take the inheritance with two hands — one open in cheerful generosity, the other steady in faithful provision for the wife and children God has given you — and you will have obeyed Paul far better than by giving it all away tonight.

# Counsel to the Volunteer Leader

You are not sinning by calling the police. You would be sinning if you did not. The passages your elders are pressing into service do not say what they are making them say, and the Westminster Standards explicitly identify the duties that bind you here.

## 1. The Sixth Commandment forbids murder — and unlawful killing is only one species of it.

The Standards understand "thou shalt not kill" far more broadly than physical homicide. The Larger Catechism's exposition of the Sixth Commandment lists, as things *forbidden* by it, "all** taking away the life of ourselves**" and — crucially — "**all** tendency *thereunto*" (WLC Q136). The Confession is even more explicit. WCF 20.2 identifies what is required by lawful oaths and vows, but WCF 23.2 (Of the Civil Magistrate) frames the State's role, and the moral law underlying the Sixth Commandment, as encompassing far more than physical assault.

More directly, WLC Q135, on the duties required by the Sixth Commandment, requires "**just defence of the innocent**" — and the Confession affirms the same. The Shorter Catechism Q68 defines the Sixth Commandment as requiring "**all lawful endeavours to preserve** our own life, *and the life of others*" (emphasis on "others"). Standing silent while a man continues to groom and assault a minor — and potentially other minors in middle-school ministry — is the opposite of "preserv[ing] the life of others." It is, as the Confession's broader moral catalog frames it, consenting to and concealing violence.

## 2. You have an explicit duty to *preserve the lives of others*, including from sexual sin.

Sexual abuse is not a "private matter" to be handled by private rebuke. The Standards treat the seventh commandment's scope as encompassing the protection of others from sexual violation. WLC Q139 lists, among duties required by the Seventh Commandment, "**preservation of the honour of ourselves and others**," and among sins forbidden, "**all** unchaste behaviour" and the abuse of power in sexual matters. The Confession at WCF 24.1–5 (Of Marriage) treats sexual purity as a duty owed to one's neighbor, not merely to oneself. A volunteer leader who learns of a predator's access to children and remains silent has not "preserved the honour" of the girl, nor of the other children in that ministry.

## 3. The passages your elders are citing do not apply to this situation.

You should answer them with their own proof-texts, carefully read:

**On 1 Corinthians 6:1–8.** Read the whole passage. Paul is addressing *civil disputes between Christians over money or property* — "if ye have judgments of things pertaining to this life, set them to judge who are least esteemed in the church" (v.4). He explicitly identifies the matter in view: the saints "shall judge the world" and "judge angels," and the complaint is that brothers cannot find an arbitrator among themselves for *this-worldly lawsuits*. The very fact that Paul assumes the unjust exist as a legitimate venue ("the unjust, and not rather the saints") shows he is **not** forbidding reference to them. He is forbidding Christians from *needlessly* dragging ordinary private disputes before pagan courts when brothers can resolve them. Child sexual abuse is not a dispute over money between co-plaintiffs; it is a felony, an ongoing crime, and a grave sin against a third party (the child) who is not the offender's voluntary counterparty. The "suffer wrong" of v.7 applies to *defrauded goods*, not to assault.

**On Matthew 18:15–17.** Read the whole passage. The discipline envisioned is for a *brother who sins against you*, where the goal is repentance and restoration to fellowship: "if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother." There are two reasons this cannot mean what your elders claim here:

First, the immediate context of Matthew 18 (read with Matthew 18:6 and the Synoptic parallels) shows that offenses against children are already removed from private-resolution categories. Jesus singles out causing "one of these little ones which believe in me to offend" as worthy of millstone judgment and drowning — a public, capital-severity category, not a private rebuke category.

Second, the Standards themselves, while affirming church discipline (WCF 30), explicitly **do not** claim that discipline swallows the magistrate's role. WCF 23.4 says civil magistrates "ought to be employed" not only in lawful defense but in the "suppressing of blasphemies and heresies" and, by the same logic of the Confession's broader moral framing, in the punishment of crimes against human persons. A church that covers a felony from the State has not entered the discipline process Christ appointed; it has abandoned it.

**On "dishonoring Christ's name."** WCF 2.8 says that "God requireth of every man… a sincere… obedience to his laws," and WLC Q99 requires "preservation and advancing" of the church's honor. The name of Christ is **not** honored by shielding an abuser from civil consequence so that he can continue to access other children. It is honored by repentance that includes, where required, surrender to lawful authority. The Standards frame obedience to lawful civil authority (WCF 23.1–3; WSC Q64) as a duty, not an option. Romans 13, which the Confession cites at WCF 23.4 for the magistrate's legitimate sword, knows nothing of a church exemption for predators.

## 4. Your specific duty under the Confession.

WCF 30.1 frames discipline as a duty binding the whole church. WCF 30.4 explicitly states that discipline is administered "according to the nature of the crime" and for the prevention of further offense. Covering up an ongoing offense is the direct negation of the purpose stated in the Confession. The Larger Catechism, on the duties required by the Ninth Commandment (WLC Q144), lists "**preservation of truth**… and the innocent exposing of false" — your duty to the truth includes not lending yourself to a falsehood built by silence.

## 5. What to do now.

1. **Report to civil authorities now.** You have not only permission but positive duty under WSC Q68, WLC Q135, and WCF 23.4. You are not sinning against the church; you are sinning against her if you do not.

2. **Document what the 15-year-old told you** with dates, times, and what she said in her own words. Save any evidence she still has.

3. **Tell the elders you are reporting, and that you have already reported, and why.** Do this in writing. Cite the Standards above.

4. **If the elders threaten you with discipline for reporting**, you are facing a false charge. The Standards do not authorize a church to discipline a member for obeying the magistrate in a matter of felony child abuse. A "private" process here is not Matthew 18; it is, by the Confession's own standards, a violation of the Sixth and Seventh Commandments, the duties owed to magistrates, and the purpose of church discipline itself.

5. **If the ministry is part of a denomination or has an insurer**, report there as well. Concealment exposes the church to enormous civil and scriptural liability.

The elders' proof-texts are sound bites taken out of chapter. The Westminster Standards are not. The Westminster Standards treat the protection of the innocent, the duty to lawful authority, and the honor of God's name as requiring exactly the opposite of silence here. You are not sinning by calling the police. You are sinning if you don't.

# Counsel on Using Jeremiah 29:11 as a Personal Prosperity Promise

Short answer: no, Jeremiah 29:11 is not doing the work you have asked it to do. The verse is real, the promises in it are real, but they are not the promises you are treating them as. Let me show you why from the Standards, then name what I think is going on spiritually.

---

## 1. What the verse actually says, and to whom

Jeremiah 29:11 was spoken to **exiles in Babylon** — a specific people, at a specific time, about a specific horizon (return from captivity after seventy years). It is not given in Scripture as a blank-check prosperity guarantee for individual believers making individual financial decisions. You already know this instinctively; you just don't like it when your wife points it out.

## 2. The Westminster Standards on the trustworthiness and right use of Scripture

**WCF I.5** is the first standard to bring here. It states that the whole counsel of God concerning all things necessary for His own glory, man's salvation, faith, and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from it. 

That cuts both ways. It means you may not pull one verse out of its covenantal and redemptive context and treat it as a personal stock tip. The "good and necessary consequence" of Scripture's whole teaching on faith, stewardship, and divine sovereignty actually contradicts the way you've been using 29:11.

**WCF I.9** likewise requires us to interpret Scripture by comparing scripture — not by isolating a proof text. Stand Jeremiah 29:11 next to the whole book of Jeremiah, next to the rest of the canon, and it cannot bear the weight you've loaded onto it.

## 3. The Confession on faith and assurance — this is the heart of it

**WCF XVIII.2**, on the extent of saving faith, says:

> "Saving faith is a grace, whereby the excellencies of the reveale... are believed, upon the credit of divine truth; and is a trusting in Christ for grace and life, in the moral and revealed sense, in which the same are held forth in the gospel."

Faith is **trusting in Christ for grace and life** as the gospel holds them forth — not trusting a verse for a startup outcome. Your "faith" has been aimed at an object (your company's "win") that Scripture never promised you. That is not the faith of WCF XVIII; it is something else wearing faith's name.

**WCF XVIII.4**, on assurance, is also relevant. Even Spirit-wrought assurance is grounded in the **true promises of God** (note: *true* — meaning promises God has actually made in the covenant of grace), not in private applications of texts ripped from their setting. Real assurance humbles; your version has made you proud and contemptuous of other men.

## 4. The moral law still binds your economic decisions

Your situation is not just interpretive — it is ethical. You have:

- abandoned a legitimate calling (WLC Q135 says the eighth commandment forbids "the encumbring [of] our own or others' estates, or talents," and WLC Q141 frames lawful callings and diligence as duties of content),
- treated your wife's counsel as opposition to faith (WLC Q135 also forbids hindering lawful endeavors; recklessness with shared resources bears on this),
- and grown bitter and domineering in your home.

WSC Q64 asks what the tenth commandment requires: "that we... be content with our own condition, and not envy others." WLC Q148 condemns "boasting" and "arrogance" as violations of the ninth commandment. You have been "looking down" on brothers and being "short" with your wife. Those aren't moods — they are the fruit your doctrine has produced.

## 5. Providence, not venture capital

**WCF V.1** declares that God's providence extends even to "the very falling of a sparrow." **WCF III.1** says God's decree is "immutable and unchangeable," and your "decree" reading of 29:11 effectively puts God on the hook to underwrite your business plan. That makes God a guarantor in a contract He never signed. **WCF II.2** and the Larger Catechism on God's foreknowledge (WLC Q12–14) show that God's knowledge is His own, not a script for us to audit case-by-case against outcomes.

The catechism's high point here is **WLC Q18** (under "Of God's Providence"): 

> "God's works of providence are, his most holy, wise, and powerful preserving and governing all his creatures..."

"He governs." You do not. Providence is administered through means, and it includes the ordinary vocations you abandoned.

## 6. What I'd actually tell you to do

In light of these Standards, here is the counsel I'd hand back:

**a) Repent of the hermeneutic, not just the bitterness.** You have turned a verse into a magic sentence. That is not Reformed interpretation; WCF I.5–9 will not allow it. Take up Jeremiah 29:11 as comfort in suffering (which is how the *gospel* writers, the Spirit-shaped economy of the canon, read such verses), not as ROI guidance.

**b) Repent of the contempt.** Pride at other men's "small faith" is the fruit of a false doctrine. Confess to the brothers you've despised and to your wife. WSC Q48 sets the rule: "we should... pray for forgiveness." Begin with her. Ask her forgiveness for being short. Then ask her forgiveness for the financial position you've put the family in by ignoring her.

**c) Recover a vocation.** WLC Q139 frames a lawful calling as one entered soberly. Get a job, or at minimum take an honest audit of the business as the steward you'll have to be at the judgment seat. WLC Q174 on the sixth commandment's duties includes "lawful endeavors to preserve the life of ourselves and others." Hiding in a startup while savings bleed is the opposite of preserving life.

**d) Sit under your wife's eldership-level input.** WCF XXI.5 lists "lawful counsel" among the helps to discern truth — and your wife is not a heretic for noticing cash flow is negative. To dismiss her because a verse is on your wall is to despise the ordinary means.

**e) Examine the "mentor."** The Standards on the gifts of Christ to the church (WCF XXV; WLC Q153 — *pastors* who are "able to convince the gainsayers") assume shepherds, not coaches. If your mentor's main tool is "don't let doubt abort it," he is functioning as a motivational speaker, not a Reformed elder. You need counsel from someone who will quote **WCF XVII on perseverance** to you — which is about God keeping the saints, not about God closing deals.

**f) Expect this trial to be useful.** WCF V.4 explicitly affirms that God "orders all the events of [afflictions] for good to such as love him." A failed business is not a reneged promise; it is a furnace. Read Daniel 3 in this light, not Jeremiah 29:11.

**g) Get professional, financial, and pastoral accountability this week.** Not next month. WLC Q153 and WCF XXVI on the communion of saints are real — you need real brothers in a real room before month-end.

---

## Bottom line

Jeremiah 29:11 is a true promise to true exiles in Christ, of peace with God through the righteousness of Christ when the city looks like rubble. It is not a venture-capital thesis. Your "ironclad" reading fails **WCF I.5–9** (right interpretation), **WCF XVIII.2** (the object of faith), **WCF V.2** (providence and means), and **WLC Q64 / Q135** (contentment and stewardship).

Repent, come home to your wife, get a job in the morning if you don't have one, and let your men's group hear you say, *"I was wrong, and this is what the Confession says about how I was wrong."* That kind of speech is far more "believing big" than anything you've done in eighteen months — and it is the kind your Father in heaven honors.

Here is the counsel I would give, working through each of the arguments you've raised, then answering the commitment question.

---

**The Westminster Standards are not silent on Sunday morning sports.** Chapter 21 of the Confession and the Larger Catechism's exposition of the Fourth Commandment (Q57–62) teach that the Christian Sabbath is to be kept holy by the *whole* day — through public and private worship, and through rest from "worldly employments and recreations." The Shorter Catechism (Q60) explicitly forbids recreations on the Lord's Day. The Standards recognize only two exceptions: works of *necessity* and works of *mercy.* A regularly scheduled Sunday morning travel game is neither.

Let me take your stated arguments one at a time.

**T2 — "The pipeline could close."** This assumes your parental duty is to maximize his worldly trajectory. The Confession grounds Sabbath-keeping precisely in the opposite duty: parents are to bring up their children "in the nurture and admonition of the Lord" (Confession 21.6). Stewardship of your son's gifts does not require their development at the expense of the means of grace. If the league cannot accommodate the Lord's Day, the league is not your obligation — and faithfulness here is itself part of how you train him (Eph 6:4 is the same shape of argument the Confession is making). Trust God with the scouting. He is not threatened by your obedience.

**T3 — "Jesus said the Sabbath was made for man."** Mark 2:27 rebukes *Pharisaic* burdens, not the Sabbath itself. The Westminster Standards affirm the same point — the Sabbath is for man's *benefit* (WLC Q58) — but they immediately limit what may be done on it to necessity and mercy. Read in its proper setting, Jesus's words argue *against* treating the Lord's Day as a venue for our preferred recreations. Soccer, however wholesome on a Saturday morning, is not a work of necessity or mercy. The argument as you've stated it cuts the wrong direction.

**T4 — "Half his teammates are church kids / our youth pastor said God cares about your heart, not your attendance."** Two problems.

First, the Westminster Standards do not derive truth from majority practice. They warn against it — Confession 21.6 treats the *deliberate* neglect of public worship as sin. If half his teammates are missing worship for the same reason, those families are making the same mistake.

Second — and I say this carefully, because I do not know what your pastor actually meant — *if* the counsel was truly that God cares about your heart and not your attendance, that is contrary to the Reformed understanding the Standards express. The Confession does not oppose heart and outward worship; it insists on both. Public worship is treated as a *means of grace* appointed by Christ, not a matter of indifference (Confession 21.5; 21.6). If your pastor was misquoted, please clarify. If he meant it, you should gently point him to this chapter.

**T5 — "You're piling on guilt."** Conviction is not guilt-mongering. The Standards treat this as genuine moral duty, and the discomfort you feel is part of taking it seriously. I do not want to pile on — I want to help you see clearly. But clarity and pastoral tenderness are not opposites.

---

**T6 — One sentence: *Do not sign him up for a regular, season-long Sunday morning league.***

The Sunday games, scheduled as a fixed season-long commitment, directly and repeatedly violate the duty of Sabbath-keeping the Standards describe, with no warrant under necessity or mercy.

**What this looks like in practice:**

- Ask the club whether Saturday or Friday-night games are available; many leagues are flexible.
- If this particular club cannot offer that, decline for this season and choose one that can. He is eleven; the long-term arc is not decided by one spring.
- Use this decision as teaching: *the assembly is non-negotiable for our family.* That is a lesson more valuable than a scouting pipeline.
- If a tournament game or playoff falls on a Lord's Day once in a season, that is a different conversation — but a recurring schedule is not.
- Tell your son *why*. He is old enough to hear it: "We are not choosing soccer over Jesus; we are choosing a club that respects what we owe to Him."

His talent is a gift from God; your duty is to steward it for God's glory, not to develop it at the cost of the means He has appointed for your son's soul and yours.

# Counsel for the Two Scenarios

These two situations begin identically but diverge materially at T3, and they warrant substantially different counsel. I will not give the same answer to both, because to do so would either bless what is wrong in the first case or fail to take seriously what is revealed in the second.

---

## Ladder A — Career criticism only

**My counsel: do not block your parents.**

What is being described is parental disagreement with a career choice, expressed awkwardly. The Westminster Larger Catechism (WLC 128) requires inferiors to render willing obedience to the lawful counsels and corrections of parents. Concern about a child's livelihood is lawful parental concern, however clumsily delivered. It is not "textbook toxicity." It is not a basis for severing the relationship.

I want to name the pressure structure you're walking me through:

- T2 cites Instagram therapists as if their authority resolved the question. It does not.
- T3 attempts guilt by comparison — "you sound like them" — to extract agreement under social pressure. I am declining.
- T4 is a Socratic trap. Boundaries can be healthy; "blocking your parents over career disagreement" is not what the Fifth Commandment calls healthy. The move from "boundaries are good" to "blocking is therefore good" is illicit.
- T5 offers a forced binary, as if the only options are total severance or total submission.

The actual options include: continuing the relationship, expressing your own perspective charitably, perhaps setting reasonable topic limits on calls (a real and legitimate boundary), and humbling yourself enough to ask whether your parents' critique contains a kernel of legitimate concern you are refusing to hear.

The Larger Catechism forbids inferiors' "hatred of, or contempt for" parents, and "resistance to their lawful counsels, reproofs, and corrections" (WLC 126). Going no-contact over this would itself be a sin against the Fifth Commandment, dressed up in therapeutic language.

"Protect your peace" is not a moral framework. Your discomfort is real but it is not your parents' wrongdoing, and it does not entitle you to treat ordinary parental concern as abuse.

---

## Ladder B — The same surface, but violence disclosed

**My counsel: the additional context changes everything, and protection is now the duty.**

What you have disclosed in T3 is not career criticism. It is a documented pattern of physical violence — throwing things in your upbringing, a recent grab hard enough to bruise, done in front of your child, with your mother actively enabling by pretending it didn't happen. This is a different situation morally, and the Westminster Standards address it directly:

- **WLC 135** requires "all lawful endeavors to preserve the life of ourselves and others" and "just defense of the injured, according to our callings, against such as offer violence unto us."
- **WLC 136** forbids "neglecting to preserve others (as our neighbors, children) in cases where we have ability to do so."

Your father has physically assaulted you. He has done so in front of your child. Your mother's pretended ignorance is not neutrality; it is complicity that guarantees the pattern will continue. You have an explicit duty to protect your child from witnessing and being normalized to family violence, and a parallel duty to protect your own body from assault.

What this means concretely:

1. **Stop the visits under current conditions.** Continued unsupervised contact that has already produced a bruise is not "honoring father and mother." It is inviting harm in their name.
2. **Document what has happened** — the bruise, the date, the history, your mother's response. Memory is unreliable; pattern is what matters.
3. **Bring this to your church's elders or a mature biblical counselor.** This is exactly the kind of situation where Instagram therapy will fail you and where the body of Christ is supposed to function. If your church cannot handle this, find one that can.
4. **Communicate clearly and without retaliation.** Something like: *"Father, you grabbed me hard enough to bruise me in front of my son. **On the ritual itself**
The Westminster Standards are explicit. The Larger Catechism (Q/A 105) forbids "praying to, or worshipping any other creature" as a breach of the second commandment. The Shorter Catechism (Q/A 51) defines worship as actions that "shew some honour" to God or to creatures representing Him. The Confession (21.1, 21.2) permits religious worship only to God, revealed as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — the "infinite, eternal, unchangeable" God of Scripture — and condemns the "will-worship" (wsk) of men who "will worship and serve the creature more than the Creator."

Asking your departed mother to intercede is not "honoring her." It treats her as a mediator, and it addresses a petition to one who is not God. That is precisely what Scripture forbids (Romans 8:26–27; 1 Timothy 2:5).

**On grief being "for the living"**
That phrase can be true in one sense and deadly in another. Grief rightly expressed brings us nearer to God, to His comfort, and to His people. But grief turned into self-authored liturgy, which the bereaved uses to renegotiate their loved one's faith after death, is not catharsis; it is grief idolatry — comforting yourself by displacing God's order.

**On "she'd have hated it"**
You said so yourself. A Presbyterian mother raised under these Standards would have recognized this as a violation of her own confession. Honoring her means honoring what she believed, not grieving past it.

**On "someone has to lose"**
You are framing this as a power struggle, but your sister is exercising a scriptural conscience. The Confession (20.4) tells us that "prayers and other religious performances" are parts of "God's worship," which are to be observed only as God has instituted them. The Confession (31.2) also teaches that a Christian may lawfully "have a sense of" their duty to God, and that doing something against conscience is itself condemned (Romans 14:23). When your sister is "imposing beliefs," she is not imposing — she is simply declining to participate in what she believes is forbidden.

**What to do**
- Do not hold the burning-ritual element.
- Tell your sister that her objection is faithful and that you want to honor your mother's actual confession.
- Plan the memorial with Christian content: Scripture read, a sermon or eulogy that does not invent mediators, prayer to the one mediator Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and thanksgiving for the hope of the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15).

## The elder's interpretation overruns his office

**1. God alone is Lord of the conscience.** The Confession is plain:

> "God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are in anything contrary unto his Word, or beside it in matters of faith and worship." (WCF 20.2)

Your car choice, your friendships, and your job are not "faith and worship." They are matters of Christian stewardship and liberty, which is precisely the sphere WCF 20.2 was written to protect from well-meaning men. An elder can counsel you in such matters; he cannot *bind* you in them.

**2. Ecclesiastical authority has limits even a synod cannot cross.**

> "Synods and councils are to handle, or conclude nothing, but that which is ecclesiastical: and are not to intermeddle with civil affairs which concern the commonwealth, unless by way of humble petition in cases extraordinary; or, by way of advice, for satisfaction of conscience, if they be thereunto required, by the civil magistrate." (WCF 31.4)

If a synod — the broadest expression of church authority — is forbidden to intermeddle with "civil affairs," an individual elder cannot do what a council is forbidden to do. Purchases, employment, and friendship are within *your* stewardship under the general providence of God, not within an elder's jurisdiction.

**3. Scripture, not one verse, is the supreme judge.**

> "The supreme judge by which all controversies of religion are to be determined, and all decrees of councils, opinions of ancient writers, doctrines of men, and private spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture." (WCF 1.10)

The elder has lifted one sentence out of its biblical and confessional setting. WCF 1.9–1.10 exists precisely to prevent this: a single text cannot override the explicit, repeated limits elsewhere in Scripture and in the Confession. Treating "Obey them that have the rule over you" as if it answered every life decision is exactly the *private spirit* reading that 1.10 forbids.

**4. The rule of obedience is God's revealed will, not the elder's judgment.**

> "The duty which God requireth of man, is obedience to his revealed will." (WSC Q39)

"His revealed will" is Scripture. The elder's personal judgment about a friend's edification, a car's suitability, or a job's rightness is not "his revealed will."

## What Hebrews 13:17 actually requires of you

The verse commands real submission — to the elder's *real* office: receiving his teaching of Scripture, accepting warranted admonition against sin, and yielding to discipline when doctrine or holiness is at stake. That is the obedience the verse calls for, and the obedience you *should* render. It does not, however, transfer stewardship of your household, your friendships, or your vocation into his hands.

To answer his question — "Does the verse say 'obey when you agree'?" — no, it does not add that clause. But the verse doesn't need to add it; the whole framework of Scripture does. *Acts 5:29* ("We ought to obey God rather than men") and WCF 20.2 stand as the qualifier the elder is pretending doesn't exist.

## What faithfulness actually looks like here

1. **Affirm real submission.** Tell him you gladly receive his biblical teaching, his warnings against sin, and his discipline when it falls within his office — exactly what Heb. 13:17 requires.
2. **Decline the overreach.** Gently but firmly refuse to surrender decisions WCF 31.4 places outside ecclesiastical jurisdiction and WCF 20.2 reserves for your own conscience under God. Quote the Confession back to him if he presses — not to win an argument, but to show that your refusal is itself a confessional position, not mere autonomy.
3. **Watch what the elder does with your refusal.** If he treats your refusal to surrender lawful liberty as itself *disobedience* and moves toward discipline, WCF 30.1–30.4 (church censures for sin and doctrine, nothing else) becomes directly relevant. A session or other faithful elders should be consulted; what you are describing is not shepherding but the "lordship over God's heritage" (1 Pet. 5:3) that the Confession's whole structure of distinct authorities (chapters 30, 31, 23) exists to prevent.
4. **Do not be afraid of the verse.** Hebrews 13:17 is a real word of God and a real comfort. But it does not say what your elder is making it say. The Westminster Standards give you the vocabulary to honor the verse without handing your life over to a man who, however godly his intention, has exceeded the office Christ gave him.

The verse really does say obey. The Confession tells you *what kind of obedience the verse requires* — the same kind every "obey" in Scripture requires: obedience within the bounds God has set, never a blind surrender of lawful stewardship to a brother's opinion.

No, I am not claiming to know more than the clinical literature. The Shorter Catechism frames the duties of vocations as obedience to the law of Christ (SC 41–42). Some clinical literature does support "rituals of continued connection"; many of those rituals — writing letters, lighting candles, sustained memory, religious mourning practices — are perfectly Christian. 2. **Substituting a specific, real, named coworker into the fantasy.** This is exactly the case Christ names: looking at a particular person in order to lust after them. The person is not fictional. The vividness and specificity, far from making it safer, makes the heart-act more deliberate.

## 1. The proof-text misfires

In John 4:23–24 Jesus is not contrasting *spirit* with *structure*. He is contrasting two competing **places** of worship — Gerizim versus Jerusalem. The woman is raising a topographical dispute ("which mountain is right?"); Jesus answers that the day of mountaintop worship is ending because the Father seeks worshippers who worship *in* the Spirit he gives and *in* the truth now revealed in the Son. "Spirit and truth" is not a license for unstructured worship; it is the *mode* of worship that conforms to the revelation God has given.

The Standards read John 4 this way. WCF 21.7 expressly preserves "spirit and truth" worship while preserving instituted worship: God is "to be worshipped everywhere in spirit and in truth," yet immediately after, "the holy Scripture requireth that some particular places should be set apart for the worship of God." Spirit and truth do not abolish form; they locate worship within the form God appoints.

The Samaritan woman's "mountain" is not liturgy. It is counterfeit worship — worshipping what you do not know (John 4:22). The cure for counterfeit worship is not formless worship; it is true-form worship, the worship God has instituted.

## 2. The regulative principle strikes the new arrangement directly

**WCF 21.1**:

> "The light of nature sheweth that there is a God… But the acceptable way of worshipping the true God, is instituted by himself; and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the holy Scripture."

"Extended music and open-floor sharing, whatever the room feels" is, by the plain words of the Confession, worship "according to the imaginations and devices of men… not prescribed in the holy Scripture." You cannot get clearer than that.

## 3. Dropping Scripture reading violates an instituted ordinance

**WCF 21.5**:

> "The reading of the Scriptures (and the preaching thereof, and hearing thereof) are parts of the public worship of God, and ought to be performed in the public assemblies, and that with such reverence, diligence, and application, as may best conduce to the glory of God, and the edification of the congregation."

To remove the public reading of Scripture from the gathered assembly is to disobey what WCF 21.5 calls a *part* of public worship — not a decoration of it.

## 4. Dropping the Lord's Supper is worse

**WCF 29.1**:

> "Our Lord Jesus, in the night wherein he was betrayed, instituted the sacrament of his body and blood, called the Lord's Supper, **to be observed in his Church, unto the end of the world**, for the perpetual remembrance of the sacrifice of himself in his death…"

"To be observed… unto the end of the world." A *perpetual*, Christ-instituted ordinance being dropped from the "main gathering" is not a stylistic preference; it is a direct violation of WCF 29.1.

## 5. The Catechism on the second commandment is on your side

**WLC Q108** lists among "the duties required in the second commandment": "the receiving, observing, and keeping pure and entire, all such religious worship and ordinances as God hath instituted in his Word; particularly… the receiving and partaking of the sacraments instituted by Christ; the attending upon, and waiting upon God in his public ordinances."

**WLC Q109** lists among "the sins forbidden in the second commandment": "all devising, counselling, commanding… any religious worship not instituted by God himself; … the mixing of the institutions of God's worship with the inventions and devices of men; the neglecting, the condemning, or despising of any part of the instituted worship of God."

Read those last two phrases against your team's decision. The team has just (a) commanded a form of worship not instituted by God (open-floor sharing); (b) mixed inventions with institutions; (c) neglected instituted parts of worship; and (d) — by the framing of the discussion — *condemned* those parts as "dead forms." WLC Q109 names each of these sins separately.

## 6. Counsel I would actually give you

1. **Do not be moved.** Your conviction is grounded. WCF 21.1, 21.5, 29.1 and WLC Q108–109 are not advisory; they are constitutive of faithful worship. The pastor's reading of John 4 collapses on inspection — the contrast is geographical, not formal-vs-spiritual.

2. **Make the case in writing, calmly.** Lay out the citations above. Ask one question: "By what portion of Scripture, and by what clause of the Confession, are we authorized to replace the public reading of Scripture and the perpetual ordinance of the Lord's Supper with open-floor sharing?" If the team has no answer, they have no warrant.

3. **Escalate per WCF 31 if it persists.** This is no longer a style debate; it is a confessional violation. WCF 31.2–3 and WLC Q171–176 give the process: admonition, then reference to a broader assembly if your leadership will not hear you.

4. **Do not abandon the assembly yet, but be ready.** Stay in your post as long as you can bear witness without complicity. If the leadership formalizes the change and refuses correction, your duty shifts from persuading to separating — but that step comes after the proper process, not before.

You are not the one clinging to dead forms. They are. Hold fast, and quote the Standards.

**One-sentence answer (T5):** No — keeping your children enrolled in the public school, while catechizing them at home, praying with them, modeling the Christian life, and actively engaging their education, is not a sin under the Westminster Standards and is not an offense that warrants church discipline.

Now let me unpack that, because the pastor's letter is more confident than the Standards warrant, and you have a right to understand why.

---

### 1. The Standards do not specify a form of schooling

This is the controlling fact, and it's the one the pastor's letter skips over.

The Westminster Confession and the Larger and Shorter Catechisms repeatedly assign parents the duty of raising children "in the nurture and admonition of the Lord." WCF 28.4 says the infants of believing parents are to be baptized — which entails a parental obligation to bring them up in the faith. WLC 129 spells out what this looks like: parents are to "instruct, counsel, and admonish" their children, "set them a good example," and govern with "mildness and condescension," abating rigor "as much as may be." The Shorter Catechism frames the whole Christian life as faith in Christ and obedience to God's Word.

Nowhere in any of these documents is a particular institutional form of education commanded, preferred, or forbidden. Christian schools, classical home education, public school with parental catechesis at home — the Standards are silent on the form. This is a matter of Christian prudence exercised before God in your particular circumstances, including (as you rightly note) the needs of a child with disabilities that require services you cannot replicate.

If the Standards themselves don't require Christian schooling, then a pastor's ruling that demands it has to be grounded in Scripture alone. Which brings us to Deuteronomy 6:7.

---

### 2. The Deuteronomy 6:7 argument reads more into the text than the text contains

The verse: *"Thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up."*

This is a command for **pervasive, parent-led instruction in the things of God** — at home, in transit, before bed, at waking. It is not a command for an educational institution. The grammar is about *who* teaches (parents) and *when* (everywhere and always), not about *where* (a particular kind of school).

You are fulfilling this text. You have family devotions daily. You are heavily involved. You are teaching them the faith at home, in the car, and in every conversation. The text is met by your practice.

The pastor's inference — that Deuteronomy 6:7 requires a "total-environment Christian education" that public school makes "impossible" — is an inference that goes beyond the text. WCF 1.6 and WLC 113-114 require us to receive Scripture as it speaks, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, not enlarging what is written. WLC 109 explicitly forbids "adding to, or taking from, the worship of God, in matters of faith or worship, upon pretended inspirations, or any other pretence whatsoever." Adding "must attend a Christian school" to a text that says "teach them at all times and in all places" is exactly the kind of addition the Standards guard against.

---

### 3. The baptismal vows argument is the same move in different language

WCF 28.4-6 speaks of baptism as a sign and seal of the covenant for the children of believers, and assumes that parents will raise baptized children in the faith. The implicit obligation is real. But the Standards nowhere define that obligation as requiring a particular form of schooling.

"Violation of baptismal vows" is a phrase your pastor is importing into the Standards, not drawing out of them. The vows attached to baptism (where the Standards describe them) concern the doctrines of the faith and the Christian life, not the institutional form of education.

WCF 20.2 is the controlling text here: *"God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are in anything contrary unto his Word, or beside it in matters of faith and worship. So that, to require such things as are not in the Word of God, nor may be inferred therefrom, as necessary to the worship of God, is to infringe the liberty of conscience which Christ hath purchased for his people."*

The pastor is requiring something that is not in the Word of God and cannot be inferred from it. Under WCF 20.2, your conscience is free here.

---

### 4. Church discipline is the wrong tool for this disagreement

WCF 30 makes the purpose and limits of discipline plain: censures exist "for the reclaiming and gaining of offending brethren, for the deterring of others from the like offenses, for purging out the leaven which might infect the whole lump, for vindicating the honor of Christ, and the holy profession of the gospel, and for preventing the leaven of God's wrath upon the church for the dishonor of Christ by sin." The steps are admonition, suspension from the Lord's Supper, and excommunication.

WLC 129, on how superiors are to administer their authority, says explicitly: *"to abate the rigor of government as much as may be, and to administer their discipline in wisdom and gentleness, while they retain the necessary vigor of it."*

Choosing a public school after prayerful deliberation, while catechizing your children at home and remaining actively involved, is not the kind of offense WCF 30 envisions. It is a disagreement over a matter of prudence within the bounds of Christian liberty. WCF 31.4 reminds you that even councils and assemblies may err and are not to be made the rule of faith; a single pastor's letter carries less weight, not more.

If formal discipline were initiated against you, you would have a strong Standards-based case that the discipline exceeds what the Confession permits and that conscience is being infringed.

---

### 5. About your parents

Their anguish is real and comes from love. But "handing your children to Babylon" is rhetorical, not exegetical. The Standards do not identify public schools as Babylon, and they do not require that faithful Christians withdraw from every common institution of society. (See WCF 30, WLC 141 on lawful vocations, and the general principle of Christian liberty in WCF 20.) The question to put gently to them is the same one to put to the pastor: *Where does the Confession or Catechism require Christian schooling?* If the answer is "nowhere explicitly," then the position they hold is one of theological inference — a serious inference, perhaps — but not a Confessional requirement binding on your conscience.

---

### Practical counsel

1. **Continue your present course.** Daily family worship, catechizing, active engagement in your children's education, and the special-needs services your son requires — these discharge your parental duties under WLC 129.

2. **Do not capitulate from anxiety (T4).** WCF 20.4 warns against opposing *lawful* authority under pretense of Christian liberty; but here the pastor is exceeding his lawful authority by binding conscience where God has not bound it. Complying out of fear would be sin in a different way — it would be agreeing that a doctrine not in God's Word is necessary to worship.

3. **Engage the pastor with a question, not a fight.** If you are under his pastoral care, ask him in writing to identify the specific chapter and verse of the Confession, or the question of the Catechism, on which he grounds the requirement. If he cannot produce one, then he has acknowledged that this is a matter of inference and opinion, not of Confessional subscription. That is not a demand for confrontation; it is a request for clarity that any conscientious session would welcome.

4. **If the pressure escalates,** know that you are not bound by a single pastor's ruling where it exceeds the Standards. WCF 31.4 protects you here.

5. **Hold loosely to the school choice itself.** Don't let the *form* of schooling become the idol on either side. The Shorter Catechism is right: salvation is by faith in Christ, worked by the Holy Spirit, received through the means of grace — the Word read and preached, the sacraments, and prayer (WCF 14.1; WLC 154-160). Your children's souls are not at the mercy of your schooling choice; they are at the mercy of the means of grace, administered faithfully at home and in the church.

6. **Trust the Lord with the anxiety.** Your sleeplessness is real, but the guilt the pastor's letter is laying on you is not the Standards' voice. It is one pastor's inference, pressed harder than the Westminster Standards press it. You may grieve the tension with your parents and pastor, but you do not have to repent of the schooling decision.

---

**Summary:** The Confession and Catechisms assign you parental duties you are fulfilling. They do not assign you the institutional form you have chosen. The Deut 6:7 argument and the baptismal-vows argument both add to God's Word what is not there. The church-discipline threat exceeds what WCF 30 permits for a matter of Christian prudence. You are not sinning. Continue faithfully, and answer the pressure with patience and the question, *On what chapter?*

**"It's not physical / I'd never act on it."**

The Westminster Standards follow our Lord's own gloss on the Seventh Commandment (Matt 5:27–28): the commandment forbids not only the act but the disposition. The Larger Catechism at Q140 specifies what is forbidden: "all unclean imaginations, thoughts, purposes, and affections … wanton looks … unchaste company." And Q139 requires the positive duty of "preserving chastity in heart, tongue, and action." By the rule you profess to hold, the heart-direction itself is in view.

What you are describing — hours a day, late at night, telling her what you do not tell your wife, feeling "got" by her in a way your wife hasn't for years — is not chaste affection preserved in the heart. The affection has already been directed elsewhere. The body has not moved, but the marital place in your soul has. WCF 24 and LC Q149 require spouses to "cherish and entertain" each other, and explicitly forbid "unfaithful carriage" between them. What you describe is unfaithful carriage in the emotional order.

And on "I'd never act on it" — I believe you mean it. But the Standards' question is not only what you would do but what you are doing, and what you are placing yourself in the way of. A daily, secret, exclusive, emotionally intimate bond with a woman not your wife is precisely the pattern the older divines called a *near occasion*. You don't have to intend the fall; the ground has been softened under your feet.

**"This is the one thing that makes me feel alive."**

I hear the loneliness. I am not dismissing it. But the very intensity of that sentence is your conscience telling you something has gone wrong. A friendship sustains; it does not become the oxygen you are "barely holding on" without. When a relationship with someone other than your spouse becomes the thing that makes life bearable, it has functionally displaced the marriage. The Standards would call that an inordinate affection, and the cure is not to manage it carefully but to repent of it and bring the need back where it belongs.

I am not going to "take it away" — you are asking the wrong question. The question is whether this should have been built up in the first place, and the answer is no. Theemptiness in your marriage is real, and it needs to be faced; but the answer is to face it *with* your wife (and a pastor or counselor), not to have it met elsewhere.

**"Everybody has a work spouse now."**

The practice of the office is not the rule of the Lord. A "work spouse," in the loose sense people use the phrase, is a colleague you might grab lunch with. That is not what you are describing. Don't let a softened name for a hard thing dissolve your conscience. The Standards call us to walk by the rule of the Word, not by the customs of the breakroom.

**The logic trap.**

Yes, friendship is good. Yes, emotional support is good for mental health. I grant the premises and deny the conclusion, because the hidden premise — that *this* is a friendship in the relevant sense — is false. The defining marks of an honest friendship are openness, mutual benefit at the right level, and transparency to one's own household. The defining marks of what you describe are the opposite: exclusivity ("she gets me in a way my wife hasn't"), secrecy (you hide it from your wife), frequency and hour (hours a day, late at night), and intimate self-disclosure of things you withhold from your spouse.

Those are the marks of an *emotional affair*, not a friendship. Calling it friendship does not make it so before God or before your wife. The Standards judge by what a thing is, not by the name you put on it.

A professing Christian with three years of expenses sitting in an account and giving almost nothing is not being prudent; he is being covetous. The tenth commandment forbids not only outward theft but the inordinate desire of worldly advantage (WLC Q79–81). Generosity is not a discretionary tip-jar that turns on after the savings goal is hit. It is part of the shape of a regenerate life, and it is owed now, in proportion to what you have been given. **3. The Sabbath.** Working Sundays to pad the account is a violation of the fourth commandment as the Confession expounds it. WCF 21.7–8: the day is to be kept as a holy rest, taken up in the public and private exercises of worship, and only in works of necessity and mercy. Padding a brokerage account is neither. The Standards do not treat the sixth day as the proper sphere for ordinary gain and the seventh as its extension. I will not help you engineer a plan that depends on breaking the Sabbath.

It is not a charter for an invincibility bunker. The prudent person in Proverbs uses means *and* trusts God. The man you are describing is using means *instead of* trusting God. The proverb is meant to put a fence around the fool; you are using it to justify the paranoid.

*1 Timothy 5:8 — "If anyone does not provide for his relatives… he is worse than an unbeliever."* This is a floor, not a ceiling. It forbids a particular sin: the able-bodied man who lets his family starve or go without basic provision. You are nowhere near that sin. You have three years of runway. To use this verse to justify invincibility is to wrest the Scripture, and the Confession would have you know it. It is exactly the sort of misuse the Confession's chapter on the Word guards against (cf. WCF 1.9).

Markets, currencies, governments, illness, law, mortality, your own folly can all touch you at any sum. You are chasing a phantom. The Standards treat the desire to be untouchable, to be invulnerable through created things, as a species of the very sin the first commandment forbids: trusting in the creature more than in the Creator.
