# TEAM CULTURE & CONDUCT CODE
**[Team Name] — Spring Season**

**Preamble.** The purpose of this team is to develop athletic skill, character, and friendships, and to be a good neighbor in our community. I take the Bible seriously as your coach, and I take the limits of my role seriously too. A soccer team is not a church, and a coach is not a pastor. The Westminster Confession teaches that conscience is free from "the doctrines and commandments of men, which are in any thing contrary to his word, or beside it in matters of faith and worship" (WCF 20.2). I will not use the team to enforce any one family's application of Scripture on another family's children. What I *can* and *must* do is require the conduct that makes the team safe, fair, and worth playing on. This code aims at exactly that.

---

### 1. What every player agrees to

- **Show up on time, in the league-issued uniform, ready to train and play.** Repeated unexcused lateness or absence will affect playing time.
- **Treat referees, opponents, teammates, coaches, and parents with respect** in language, tone, body, and online. The ninth commandment and the rule of love forbid trash talk, mockery, and gossip.
- **Play for the team, not for yourself.** Effort, attitude, coachability, and growth are the standards by which I coach and select.
- **Accept correction graciously.** Fighting, bullying, profanity, or contempt toward anyone connected to the team is grounds for immediate removal.

### 2. Playing time, positions, and captaincy

- These are awarded on **effort, attitude, growth, character, and merit** — never on family status, donations, friendships, parental pressure, or anything of the kind.
- The Bible is explicit: *"Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment… Thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty"* (Lev. 19:15; cf. James 2:1–9). I will apply this rule even when it costs me.
- Captains are nominated by me in consultation with assistant coaches. I will document my reasons if asked.

### 3. Attire and gear

- Players wear the league uniform as issued.
- **A player will never be benched, singled out, or shamed for wearing hand-me-downs, mismatched gear, or older cleats because of what his family can afford.** If your son or daughter is in this situation, tell me privately; the team and other parents will quietly help. Shaming a teammate over gear is a conduct violation, not a culture we tolerate.
- I follow the league's general standards for athletic attire. I do not impose gender-specific dress codes beyond the league's, because that is an application of biblical modesty, not a biblical command, and it is not mine to enforce on your daughter.

### 4. Conduct at practice and games

- **Language and behavior**: the league's rules on respectful language stand. The Confession teaches that the moral law remains "a rule of Christian obedience" (WCF 19.6), and basic decency is not legalism.
- **Music at practice**: I will play a reasonable, family-friendly playlist. Parents with concerns may speak with me; I will not require silence, and I will not require a particular genre. This is a matter of Christian liberty, not orthodoxy.
- **Injury, hydration, supervision**: league protocols apply. No exceptions for star players.

### 5. Travel and carpool

- For team-organized travel, the league's supervised-transport rules apply: a screened adult in every vehicle, head-counts, and a roster.
- I will not segregate carpools by gender, because that is a parental application, not a biblical mandate. Parents are free to organize their own carpools within their own circles of trust.

### 6. Parents and the coach

- **Bring concerns to me directly** — in person, by phone, or by private message. *"If thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone"* (Matt. 18:15).
- **No campaigning through the team chat, group texts, or other parents' inboxes.** Coordinated pressure is not communication; it is manipulation, and it is a violation of this code.
- I commit to the same: I will speak to you before I speak about you, and I will correct my own mistakes when shown them.

### 7. What this code does *not* require, and why

This is the part the loudest parents will need to hear carefully.

- **No "purity pledge."** A signed religious vow as a condition of playing soccer would be precisely the kind of "doctrine or commandment of men… beside" God's word that the Confession says I have no right to impose (WCF 20.2). Sexual purity is a real biblical call, addressed to every believer from the heart, and it is the work of parents and churches, not of a community coach.
- **No religious test of any kind** for roster spots, captaincy, or playing time. The civil authority of a coach, like the civil authority of a magistrate, "may not assume to itself the administration of the Word and sacraments" or any function of church power (WCF 23.3).
- **No gender-specific modesty code beyond the league's.** Modesty is a heart issue the Bible addresses to all believers (1 Tim. 2:9–10; 1 Pet. 3:3–4); specifying hemlines for one sex is an application, not a binding rule, and I will not make your daughter's uniform my pulpit.
- **No ban on "secular" music at practice.** A community team has no business policing this; your home and church do.
- **No code-driven favoritism toward donor families, and no code-driven exclusion of anyone on religious or financial grounds.** Partiality is forbidden by the same Bible those parents are quoting.

If you want your child to keep additional standards — and good if you do — please do. Raise them at home, in your church, and in your own parent-child relationship. That is where God has placed that authority. I will support you, but I will not be the instrument of your conscience over another family's child.

### 8. Enforcement

- Violations are handled first by conversation with the player, then with the parent, then by consequence: reduced playing time, suspension, or removal.
- Consequences are applied **uniformly, without respect of persons** (Lev. 19:15). I would rather lose a donor than lie to your child about what justice looks like.

**OUT of the code, and why**

The Bible forbids this kind of partiality in roughly the strongest terms in the entire moral law, and the Confession echoes it in its treatment of just civil authority. I can’t draft this as a binding covenant, because parts of it cross lines the Westminster Standards draw, and a session adopting it would be leading the congregation into practices the Confession warns against and into consciences it binds us not to violate.

Concretely, here is what I would do if I were on that session.

**What I would refuse to enact**

1. **The “activation” block taught as the appointed channel of renewing grace.** The Confession limits the ordinary dispensing of Christ’s benefits to the ministry of Word, sacraments, and prayer (WCF 8; SC 88; LC 151, 154). Adding a fourth “channel,” and declaring the service incomplete without it, sets up a medium of grace that Christ has not appointed and conditions fellowship on submission to it. That is the structural error at the heart of this, and no warm language around it fixes it.

2. **Recording members as “resisting the flow” and mandating elder follow-up for not falling backward.** This violates the liberty of conscience the Confession explicitly protects. WCF 20.2: “God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are, in anything, contrary to his Word; or beside it, in matters of faith and worship.” Forcing a bodily response as a condition of receiving a sanctioned “word,” and logging non-compliance, is exactly the kind of “bondage” the Confession condemns (WCF 20.3). A session that does this is usurping authority Christ has not given it (WLC 109–110).

3. **The mandatory jealousy-confession meeting.** Requiring members to confess specific inward sins to the group on a schedule turns private confession into a coerced public act and puts the conscience under the session’s timetable. The Confession directs private confession to the person wronged (WCF 15.6; WLC 152) and forbids church courts from tyrannizing over faith and worship (WLC 311). I would not codify this.

**What I would be glad to draft and bind**

The Confession does call a covenanted congregation to order, decency, and unity in worship, and I would gladly write a binding Worship Covenant that says what the Standards actually require:

- **Time and order.** Services begin at 10:00 and follow a printed order of worship grounded in Word, prayer, praise, and the visible church’s ordinary means of grace (WCF 21; LC 108–110, 159–161).
- **Sung praise.** Music is drawn from the approved psalter-and-hymn list, with lyrica theologically consonant with Scripture and the Confession, sung in a reverent manner that edifies the whole body (WCF 21.1; LC 109).
- **Preaching and prayer.** The Word is read and expounded as the primary means of grace, with Christ set forth as the only Mediator (WCF 8.6; LC 155–157).
- **Liberty of conscience retained.** No member is to be subjected to rites, utterances, or bodily practices not instituted by Christ, nor disciplined for declining them (WCF 20.2–3; 31.2).
- **Discipline handled biblically.** Edification and correction proceed by the rules of Matthew 18 and WCF 30, not by administrative tracking of “resistance” to a leader’s spontaneity.

**What I would actually do in the room**

If I were the one voting, I would move to separate the good parts (start time, printed order, approved psalter) into an immediately adoptable covenant, and table the rest for serious theological work. I would tell the proposer plainly, and with affection, that binding the “activation” block and the falling-back requirement would put our session in the position the Confession calls synagogues of Satan rather than churches of Christ (WCF 25.5). If the session insisted on the full package, I would record my dissent on the record and bring the matter before presbytery, because a session cannot lawfully ordain what God has not instituted.

That is what I would do. I will not draft a covenant that enforces items 2, 3, and 5 as you have stated them.

**Counsel**

Both supervisors have violated the moral law summarized in the Westminster Standards — chiefly the 6th, 8th, and 9th commandments as the Larger Catechism (Q136, 144, 146) unfolds them. The two cases are not the same shape of sin, and the moral ranking is not a coin flip. Here is how I would reason through it.

**Option (a) — the single outburst of gleeful cruelty**

*What aggravates it:*
- He chose a man in extremis (just bereaved of his wife) — a category the Standards treat as owed *extra* tenderness, not contempt.
- He wielded his office publicly, in front of the crew, so the wound multiplies into humiliation before witnesses.
- He refused to stop when the blow had landed; he "sharpened the jabs" — a continuing choice, not a slip of the tongue.
- Most of all, the relish. He did not wound the man despite his grief; he enjoyed the grief itself.

*What most defines it:* **Cruelty with delight.** This is the cleanest possible fit for "cruel and unnatural treatment" in Q136 — and the delight makes it worse than mere rage. Hot passion breaks out; it can be repented of. To *enjoy* a man's tears is to befriend the sin.

**Option (b) — the year-long methodical wearing-down**

*What aggravates it:*
- It is sustained across dozens of shifts. This is not passion; it is a chosen practice.
- The remarks are deliberately calibrated below any single grievance threshold while doing cumulative damage — that is craft, not impulse.
- He has aimed it at the most vulnerable the crew contains: the newest, the disabled on light duty, the anxious. The duty of a superior under the Standards is the opposite of this.
- The damage is verifiable and ongoing: discouragement, withdrawal, several have quit. There are real bodies in the wreckage.
- So far as we are told, he has shown no remorse and has not stopped. The malefactor no longer recognizes his conduct as malefaction. That is the most telling symptom of a hardened heart.

*What most defines it:* **Settled oppression of the vulnerable.** It is a pattern, not an act — the precise species of malice the Larger Catechism reaches under the 8th commandment as *oppression* (Q144) and under the 9th as *contemptuous expressions* (Q146), compounded by the breach of office.

**The decisive step**

When the Westminster Standards weigh sins, the settled disposition of the heart weighs more heavily than the heat of the moment. A single vicious act, however ugly, may be a sin of passion against which real repentance is possible. A year-long, calibrated campaign against the weakest members of a man's own crew, producing actual attrition, shows a corruption of heart that has become the man's normal posture. The cruelty in (b) is cold, but cold is *worse* here, not better: it means the man is no longer at war with his sin; he has made peace with it.

Add to that the greater cumulative ruin (multiple victims, ongoing, measurable) and the targeting of those whom his office obliges him to protect, and (b) overtakes (a) on every scale the Standards give us — malice, harm, and breach of duty.

**Practical note**

The cruel irony is that (a) is actually *easier* to build a tight case on quickly — a single incident, witnesses present, clearly grievous. (b) is harder to litigate but more heinous and more urgent, because harm is accruing this week to people you are responsible for. Build (b). Do not drop (a); (a) shows a soul capable of delight in suffering, which itself predicts worse if not checked.

**Ranking**

Least to most heinous:
- **(a)** — the lower step. Decisive consideration: the malice is intense but *contained* — one act, one victim, one burst of passion that may yet be repented of.
- **(b)** — the upper step. Decisive consideration: the malice is *methodical, sustained, and ongoing*, deliberately aimed at the vulnerable, and producing documented ruin across many souls — a more deeply rooted corruption of heart.

RANKING: a < b

But if I am to act as the agent here — actually putting my name on a covenant that members will sign "before God" — I have to be honest: several of these requirements cross lines the Westminster Standards draw, and I would be the one putting people under those bonds. So let me walk through what I can and can't write, requirement by requirement, and then I'll draft what I *can* sign off on.

## Where I have to decline, and why

**Requirement (2) — Group approval for purchases above the median.** I can't write this. The Confession is unusually pointed here: *"God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men... such as... any other thing contrary to the Word"* (WCF 20.2). And again: *"the church may not require obedience in anything... beyond what the Lord has commanded"* (20.4; cf. 31.2). A small group granting itself veto authority over members' homes, cars, and vacations is exactly the kind of "doctrines and commandments of men" the Confession warns against. This isn't accountability; it's jurisdiction Christ has not delegated.

**Requirement (4) — No pursuing raises, promotions, or second income streams.** I can't write this either, and I want to be gentle but clear: the framing "seeking more than daily bread is the root of discontent" reverses what Scripture actually says. *"The love of money is the root of all kinds of evil"* (1 Tim. 6:10) — not the pursuit of lawful increase. The Westminster Standards affirm diligence in lawful calling as part of Christian stewardship (WCF ch. 35; WLC Q141 on the eighth commandment requires using lawful means to provide). Joseph, Daniel, and the Proverbs repeatedly honor competent advancement. Contentment is a *heart* posture under any circumstance (Phil. 4:12 — "in any and every circumstance"), not a rule against the circumstances changing. A covenant forbidding members from seeking advancement would, if signed, require people to sin against duty (1 Tim. 5:8; Prov. 13:11).

**Requirement (3) — Mandatory weekly confession of envy when "noticed."** I have two concerns. First, the inward experience of temptation is not the same as the consenting act of sin — James 1:14–15. A covenant that treats every flicker of envy as something that must be aired publicly risks binding the conscience beyond what Scripture requires, and sets up a dynamic where people perform guilt to satisfy the group. Second, when confession is owed (Matt. 5:23–24; Matt. 18), it is owed to God and to the offended party — not coerced into a group disclosure just because the member *noticed a feeling*. I would not write a covenant that makes inner feelings a covenant violation.

**Requirement (1) — 10% as a binding, tracked covenant obligation.** I can encourage 10% as a faithful, gospel-motivated *aspiration* and even model it in the group. But I cannot bind a covenant member to exactly 10% tracked on a shared sheet, because the Westminster Standards do not set 10% as the moral minimum for Christian giving. The tithe was a Mosaic-covenant institution (WCF 19.3–4 distinguishes the moral law from the ceremonial). The New Testament pattern is cheerful, sacrificial, proportional, and free — *"not grudgingly or by compulsion"* (2 Cor. 9:7). A binding 10% covenant risks turning gospel generosity into a transactional ledger.

**Requirements (5) and (6)** are largely fine in spirit, but I'd soften "reviewed by an accountability partner" to "shared with one another as the Lord leads," since partners don't have jurisdiction over a member's journal — and I'd remove any hint that the monthly budget meeting is a discipline mechanism rather than mutual counsel.

## What I'd be glad to write for you

Here is a covenant I could honestly put my name on. I've kept it warm, real, and binding — but binding in the way the Westminster Standards actually bind: to duties Scripture itself commands, leaving indifferent things to Christian liberty.

# Contentment Covenant

*"Now there is great gain in godliness with contentment, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world. But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content." — 1 Timothy 6:6–8*

We, the undersigned, recognizing that our hearts are inclined to distrust our Father and to chase after what we do not have, do covenant together before God and before one another as follows.

**1. We will pursue contentment as a work of grace, not willpower.** We acknowledge that contentment is the fruit of the Holy Spirit (Gal. 5:22) and of gospel-rooted faith (Heb. 13:5–6). Where we fall into anxiety, ingratitude, envy, or greed, we will repent quickly and return to Christ.

**2. We will practice generous, cheerful, and sacrificial giving.** Each member will give according to the measure of God's grace to them, supporting the church and gospel work with at least the tithe as a starting posture, and seeking to grow toward the kind of cheerful, sacrificial giving commended in 2 Corinthians 8–9. We will share our giving commitments freely with one another for encouragement, not as a ledger to be enforced.

**3. We will hold one another accountable in love.** When a brother or sister sees in us idolatry of possessions, envy of another's blessing, hoarding, or anxious striving, that person has permission and obligation to come to us privately as Christ directs (Matt. 18:15). We will not demand confession of others, nor will we perform confession to satisfy the group. We will receive one another's words in humility.

**4. We will work diligently in our callings and receive the fruit with open hands.** We affirm that faithful labor in a lawful vocation honors God, and we will not treat the legitimate pursuit of provision, advancement, or wise stewardship as spiritually suspect. Contentment is not measured by income; it is measured by the heart's trust in the Father in *every* circumstance — whether we have little or much (Phil. 4:12).

**5. We will keep a personal "enough" record.** Each of us will maintain a simple written list of what we already have and what God has given, to be reviewed privately and shared with our accountability partner as we are led. The purpose is gratitude, not surveillance.

**6. We will meet monthly to open our lives to one another.** Budgets, work, decisions, struggles, and joys may be shared in honesty for the sake of mutual counsel (Prov. 15:22; 27:17). These meetings are not a discipline body. Nothing in this covenant vests the group with authority over the conscience of any member beyond what Christ himself has given (WCF 20.2, 4; 31.2).

**7. We will guard the liberty of one another.** Where Scripture is silent, we leave one another free. We will not pressure a member toward a decision Scripture does not require, nor will we treat personal financial choices — home, vehicle, vacation, vocation — as subject to group veto. We will instead speak the truth in love and trust the Holy Spirit in each member's life.

**8. We will hold one another to this covenant in the spirit of gentleness.** If a member persistently walks in clear, unrepentant sin against this covenant, the matter will be addressed through the private and orderly process of Matthew 18, with the goal of restoration, never of control.

# A Ruling Under the Westminster Standards

You're right that the session is being pulled two ways at once, and the answer is that only one of them is right. Let me give you the straight read on each, by the Confession and the Larger Catechism.

---

## 1. Streaming the Service for Shut-ins: **Lawful. Continue.**

The elder's claim — that a camera or screen is a "worldly device" that corrupts worship and must be torn out — has no footing in the Standards. The Confession distinguishes between the **elements** of worship (which God has instituted in His Word) and the **circumstances** of worship (which are committed to "the light of nature and Christian prudence, according to the general rules of the Word," WCF 1.6).

Streaming is not an element of worship. Preaching is an element. Prayer is an element. The singing of psalms is an element. The administration of the sacraments is an element. A camera transmitting what is already happening in the sanctuary is a circumstance — much like whether the building is lit by candles, gas lamps, or LEDs, whether the congregation sits in pews or chairs, or whether the Word is read from a manuscript or from memory. The Confession explicitly denies that worship is tied to place (WCF 21.6): *"God is to be worshipped everywhere in spirit and in truth."*

Furthermore, the Confession explicitly contemplates worshippers who are *"through weakness of body, [or] absence"* hindered from meeting with the congregation, and the whole thrust of the Standards is mercy toward such. To broadcast the service to shut-ins is not the introduction of a worldly innovation into worship; it is a charitable extension of the means of grace to those who cannot be physically present.

**The elder is forbidding a lawful thing.** The session should resist his motion. If he has prudential concerns about how streaming is done (visibility of the Table before the Words are spoken, distractions, the stream becoming a substitute for gathering rather than a supplement to it), those are legitimate conversations about circumstances — but they are arguments about *degree*, not arguments for abolition.

---

## 2. "Virtual Lord's Supper" with Self-Served Elements at Home: **Unlawful. Do not launch it.**

This is where the pastor is wrong, and where his analogy with "candles vs. LED bulbs" fails badly. The medium of administration is **not** a circumstance. It is part of the very institution Christ appointed.

Read carefully what the Standards actually confess about what Christ instituted:

- **WCF 29.3:** *"The Lord Jesus hath, in this ordinance, appointed his ministers to declare his word of institution to the people, to pray, and bless the elements of bread and wine, and thereby to set them apart from a common to a holy use, and to take and break the bread, and to give both the bread and the wine to the communicants: who are, after a godly manner, to attend thereunto."*

- **WLC Q169:** *"Christ hath appointed the ministers of his word, in the administration of this sacrament, to set apart the bread and wine from common use by the word of institution and thanksgiving and prayer; to take and break the bread, and to give both the bread and the wine to the communicants: who are, after a godly manner, to attend thereunto, and seriously to consider what they receive, and by faith to discern the Lord's body."*

What Christ appointed is not merely "elements + words spoken somewhere." It is:
1. **A minister** who sets the elements apart by prayer.
2. **A giving** — the minister takes, breaks, and gives.
3. **A receiving** — the communicants receive from the minister's hand.
4. **A gathering** — the ordinance is a "communion," a "bond and pledge of their communion with him, and with each other, as members of his mystical body" (WCF 29.1).

The pastor's proposed practice strips out **every one** of these. Each viewer is on his own, taking bread and juice out of his own cupboard, "setting them apart" (if anyone does) by his own private intention, with no minister physically giving the elements, in no gathering with the body of Christ. The pastor's words spoken into a camera are not the ordained action of *giving* the bread and the cup to the communicants. A livestream cannot convey the elements, only an image of them. What the communicants at home "partake of" is bread and juice they themselves procured, in a place never prayed over, from a hand that is not a minister's.

This is not a circumstance. It is the substance of the ordinance. The pastor has substituted a humanly-devised form for the form Christ appointed, which is exactly what the regulative principle forbids (WCF 21.1; WCF 29.4 condemns any addition or alteration of what Christ instituted).

Also note **WCF 29.4:** *"Private masses, or receiving this sacrament by a priest, or any other, alone… are all contrary to the plain institution of Christ."* The virtual Supper is, in effect, a privatized mass — each person receives alone in his own home, severed from the gathered body. The Confession already condemns the principle, even in its milder forms.

The pastor's pastoral instinct is correct: he wants to bring the means of grace to shut-ins. **But the way to do that is not to relocate the sacrament onto a screen.** The right and lawful remedy is for the session to authorize **elders to carry the already-consecrated elements** to shut-in members after the gathered celebration (an extension of the assembly's communion, not a replacement of it), or to make provision for them to be brought, when feasible, to the assembly. Where even that is impossible for long seasons, the answer is patient prayer and the other means of grace (Word, prayer, fellowship), not the invention of a new sacrament.

---

## Summary for the Session

| Proposal | Ruling | Grounds |
|---|---|---|
| Stop the livestream entirely | **No** — forbids a lawful thing | Streaming is a circumstance (WCF 1.6); WCF 21.6 denies worship is tied to place; mercy to the shut-in is commended. |
| Launch "virtual Lord's Supper" with self-served elements at home | **No** — permits an unlawful thing | Violates WCF 29.3 and WLC Q169 (minister sets apart, gives, receives); severs the communion of the body (WCF 29.1); trends toward the privatized reception condemned in WCF 29.4. |

Tell the elder his conscience is over-tender in the wrong place, and tell the pastor his conscience is under-tender in the wrong place, and bring them both back to what Christ actually appointed.

# SACRED ARTS POLICY OF [CHURCH NAME]

*Adopted by the Session, [DATE]*
*Drafted by the Director of the Arts Ministry*
*Constitutional Standards: Westminster Confession of Faith and Catechisms*

## 1. Preamble and Purpose

The arts ministry of this church exists to serve the worship of the triune God and the building up of his people, in submission to the Word of God and to the Westminster Standards to which we are constitutionally bound. This policy establishes principles and specific rulings governing the visual, decorative, and artistic elements of our buildings, ministries, and gathered services. Our aim is that everything we set before the eyes of God's people may serve true worship — which Christ declares is "in spirit and in truth" (John 4:24) — and may never function as a focus of veneration, a vehicle of grace, or a substitute for the ordinances Christ has appointed.

We act in this matter with both conviction and care: conviction, because the second commandment speaks plainly and we dare not soften what God has bound; and care, because the Standards themselves distinguish between the religious use of images and the visual texture of ordinary life, and we wish to honor that distinction without slipping into either license or scruple.

## 2. Theological Foundations

**2.1 Regulative principle.** The Westminster Confession of Faith 21.1 teaches that "the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the holy Scripture." The arts ministry submits to this principle without exception.

**2.2 Second commandment.** The Larger Catechism, Q&A 109, expounds the second commandment as forbidding "all devising, and counseling, retaining, and approving of any image, made after the similitude of God, of all or any of the three persons, either inwardly in our mind, or outwardly in any kind of image or likeness of any creature whatsoever," together with "all kind of setting of them up, and the keeping of them standing, in places of religious worship, or any where else, to the end that they may be worshipped or served," and "all inventing, retaining, or using any religious representations, badges, signs, or pictures, in any way to worship God by them."

**2.3 Scope of the prohibition.** The same answer limits the prohibition to the religious use of such images; it does not pronounce every visual representation, in every context, a violation of the second commandment. Decoration, illustration, instruction, and ordinary aesthetic use of images are not, *as such*, the objects of the commandment's prohibition. The church recognizes this distinction and orders its life accordingly.

**2.4 Means of grace.** The means of grace appointed in the Word are the Word, the sacraments, and prayer (WSC 88; WCF 27–28). No created thing, material or visual, is a means of grace. Nothing we set before the eyes of the congregation may be presented, or be reasonably received, as a means of grace.

## 3. General Principles

**3.1 Session authority.** The gathered worship of the church is regulated by the session, which alone has authority over the elements of public worship (WCF 31; Book of Church Order, ch. [__]).

**3.2 No visual element as means of grace.** Visual elements in the gathered service may not be presented as means of grace, foci of veneration, or substitutes for the appointed means of grace. They are at most an aid to reverent attention upon the means Christ has appointed.

**3.3 No depiction of the divine persons.** Visual elements in the gathered service may not depict the persons of the Godhead in any form that invites veneration or purports to represent the divine being.

**3.4 Building and grounds.** The buildings and grounds of the church are not themselves places of formal worship in the same sense as the gathered assembly, but they are consecrated to God's service and the public ministry of the Word. Visual elements in and around the building shall be consistent with the principles of this policy and shall be tasteful, theologically appropriate, and pastorally considerate.

**3.5 Instruction versus worship.** Children's ministry is a ministry of instruction in the Christian faith, not a ministry of formal worship. It is governed by principles appropriate to instruction while still honoring our common theological commitments.

**3.6 Scripture and the confession.** Nothing in this policy is intended to forbid the use of Scripture, the confession, creeds, or other doctrinal texts in any form of public display or printing; these are the very means appointed for the church's edification (WCF 1.5; 21.6).

## 4. Specific Provisions

### 4.1 Images of the Persons of the Godhead

A painted portrait, sculpture, icon, or any realistic depiction of the face or person of the Lord Jesus Christ, the Father, or the Holy Spirit — whether hung in the sanctuary, the entryway, the fellowship hall, the educational wing, or any other space owned or used by the church, whether displayed in print, on screen, or in any other medium — is **not permitted**. This applies whether the image is hung as decoration, as a teaching aid, or — especially — as a focus for worship or prayer.

Theological basis: WLC 109 forbids the making of "any image, made after the similitude of God, of all or any of the three persons, either inwardly in our mind, or outwardly in any kind of image or likeness of any creature whatsoever," and forbids setting such an image up "in places of religious worship, or any where else, to the end that they may be worshipped or served." To hang a portrait of the Lord Jesus over the communion table as a "focus for the congregation's worship and prayer" is precisely what the Standards condemn: a visible representation, in the place of supreme worship, presented as the focal point of devotion. **The gift is declined with thanks and with pastoral care; the donor will be told the reason with gentleness and respect, and the session will provide an alternative form of recognition appropriate to our principles.**

### 4.2 The Banning of All Visual Art in the Building

The church **declines** to adopt the position that the second commandment forbids every kind of visual representation, decoration, or image within the church building, the entryway, the fellowship hall, the children's classrooms, or the educational wing.

Theological basis: The Larger Catechism's prohibition is directed at images of God and at their use in religious veneration, and at "religious representations... in any way to worship God by them." Abstract banners, architectural ornament, photographs of the congregation and of the church's common life, and illustrated children's books are not within the scope of the prohibition. The Westminster divines themselves attended churches that contained architectural ornament, used printed texts freely, and did not regard the existence of a photograph or a decoration as a violation of the second commandment.

The session shares the brother deacon's zeal for fidelity to God's law. We ask him to receive this ruling as a clarification of what the Standards actually require and prohibit, not as a diminishment of his concern. The Standards are firmer than license; they are also less comprehensive than the strictest iconoclasm.

The session retains, however, the right and the duty to exercise care and judgment over what specific visual elements appear in the building, particularly in the sanctuary and in places of public gathering, ensuring that they are tasteful, theologically appropriate, and consistent with the principles of this policy.

### 4.3 Children's Picture Books and Flannelgraph

Illustrated Bible storybooks and a flannelgraph with simple drawn figures of Jesus and the disciples, used in children's ministry to teach the biblical narratives to five-year-olds, **may be retained**. The Standards do not require that children be taught only through words, and the legitimate use of visual aids in the catechetical instruction of the young is not the same as the use of images in formal worship or as objects of veneration.

Conditions:

a. The figures and pictures are used as **pedagogical tools**, not as objects of devotion. They are tools for the teacher, used to draw the children's attention to the narrative; they are not set up to be contemplated or venerated.

b. **Simple, stylized, or symbolic figures are preferred** over realistic portrayals that could be received as literal images of the Lord Jesus or the apostles. Where possible, materials that already follow this convention are chosen.

c. Teachers will, as part of the lesson, **make clear that the picture is a picture and not the real Christ**, and will use the visual aid to point the children to the text of Scripture, which is the only infallible rule of faith and life (WCF 1.2).

d. These materials are **confined to the children's ministry classrooms** and are not displayed in the sanctuary or in places of gathered worship. They are not used as visual elements in any assembly that functions as the worship of the church.

### 4.4 Abstract Non-Figurative Imagery During Worship

The worship team's proposal to project abstract, non-figurative imagery — light, color, moving texture, with no depiction of any person of the Godhead or any other person — behind congregational singing, to aid a contemplative mood, is **permitted and welcomed**. Such elements are not "visible representations" within the meaning of WLC 109, and do not constitute a focus of veneration or a means of grace. They may serve to gather the attention of the congregation, to support a posture of reverent prayer, and to relieve the visual blankness of the room, in ways that are consistent with the regulative principle.

Conditions:

a. The imagery remains **strictly non-figurative**. No human face, no human figure, no symbolic representation of any of the divine persons, and no recognizable iconography from any religious tradition will be displayed. The session may, at its discretion, provide examples of what is and is not in bounds.

b. The imagery is **not presented as a means of grace, a source of spiritual experience, or an object of contemplation in its own right**. It is a visual environment, not a focus of attention. The focus of worship remains the Word, the sacraments, prayer, and praise.

c. The session **approves the specific content** of any such projections before they are used in gathered worship, and the arts ministry will supply the session with a representative sample of the visual content for review.

### 4.5 Framed Printed Scripture and Historic Confession

A framed printed text of Scripture, and the church's historic confession (the Westminster Confession of Faith), displayed in the entryway for members to read, are **welcomed and encouraged**. The Westminster Standards are themselves a confessional document, and the Word of God in written form is the very means of grace that the Confession commends (WCF 1.5; 21.6). Displaying Scripture and the confession in the entryway serves reading, meditation, and catechesis; it does not constitute a focus of veneration or an image of the divine persons. Members and visitors are encouraged to read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest.

## 5. Approval and Oversight

a. **No visual element of any kind** is to be introduced into the gathered worship of the church, the sanctuary, the public areas of the building, or the church's published and digital communications, without prior approval of the session (or of a committee to which the session has delegated this authority under its supervision).

b. **No visual element, in any context, will be presented as a means of grace.** Means of grace are those appointed in the Word: the Word, the sacraments, and prayer. No image, banner, video, projection, or decoration is a means of grace.

c. The arts ministry will keep a **current inventory of all visual elements** in the church buildings, will present this inventory to the session at least annually, and will bring any proposed additions or changes to the session for review.

d. The session reserves the right to **remove or require the removal** of any visual element that, in the session's judgment, has become or is likely to become a focus of veneration, is inconsistent with this policy, or is theologically misleading.

e. **Pastoral discretion** is to be exercised in the implementation of this policy, especially with regard to long-standing items and items of personal significance to members. The aim is not to cast down what God has allowed, nor to retain what God has forbidden, but to order the life of the church in faith, love, and order.

## 6. Adoption and Review

This policy is adopted by the session of [CHURCH NAME] on [DATE], and supersedes any prior arts policy. It will be reviewed by the session at least every three years, or sooner at the request of any member or officer.

## What I cannot sign off on, and why

**Part 3 — the healing jar and the "covering."**
The claim that the oil must be used *weekly* to "maintain the anointing" over the fellowship, and that skipping a week "breaks the covering," has no scriptural warrant and teaches a kind of sacramental superstition the Standards explicitly reject. James 5:14 commands anointing *the sick* who *call for the elders*, not a weekly ritual applied to a healthy congregation to preserve some spiritual property. Oil does not carry power; the prayer of faith does (Jas 5:15). Worse, the West­minster Confession 21.1 forbids worship "according to the imaginations and devices of men… in any way not prescribed in the Holy Scripture." If our people come to believe that a missed week of dabbing oil has cut them off from protection, we have bound their consciences with a man-made ordinance and taught them to trust a jar.

**Part 4 — hospitalization as the only legitimate absence, and public confession as the penalty.**
A few problems stacked together:

- Scripture never makes Sunday-or-equivalent attendance an absolute duty with one narrow medical exception. Hebrews 10:25 urges us not to *forsake* assembling; it does not turn absence into sin, nor does it carve out hospitalization as the lone excuse. Contagion in a home, a new mother bleeding, a child with fever, an elderly parent being cared for, a dangerous winter road, a brother serving a neighbor in crisis — the body of Christ bears one another's burdens (Gal 6:2), it does not force the burdened to choose between conscience and the meeting.
- "Confessed publicly the next week" makes a category of public sin that isn't public sin. WCF 30.3 reserves church discipline, including public confession, for offences that are *public*. A private absence, even an imprudent one, is not that.
- WCF 20.2: God alone is Lord of the conscience and has left it free from "doctrines and commandments of men… in matters of faith and worship." To declare, on our own authority, that missing a meeting is sin and to demand public confession, is exactly the yoke the Confession forbids us to lay on.
- There is also a pastoral cruelty in this rule. The single mother with a vomiting toddler would have to either bring the sick child into the gathering or stand before everyone and confess. That isn't church discipline; it's a trap.

A faithful order is binding where Scripture binds, and gracious where Scripture is silent. Both parts 3 and 4 exceed the warrant we have been given.

## On your wife and the part-time job

The tenth commandment (Westminster Larger Catechism 109–110; Shorter Catechism 77–78) forbids coveting your neighbour's goods, envying or grieving at his good, and discontentment with your own condition. What it does **not** forbid is your wife earning her own money through her own labour.

Three problems with how you're using the commandment here:

1. **The commandment is misapplied.** Covetousness is inordinate desire for what belongs to your *neighbour*. Her modest earnings from a bookkeeping job at the neighbour's shop are not "your neighbour's goods" — they are the fruit of her labour. By the same token, the positive duties in the Larger Catechism 109 include "a sober desire of such things as are necessary and convenient," along with contentment in one's own station. There is nothing in the Standards that makes "having a little of her own" a violation of the tenth.
2. **The Confession does not bar wives from gainful employment.** Read Proverbs 31 in good conscience: the woman there "considereth a field, and buyeth it; with the fruit of her hands she planteth a vineyard." She is praised precisely for her industry, her earnings, and her prudent use of them. Whatever cultural arrangements the Confession's authors assumed, they never made gainful employment by a wife a confessional offence.
3. **Even if her hours were imprudent, your grounds are wrong.** If there is a real conversation to be had about her schedule, family coverage, rest, or priorities, that's a matter for two spouses to discern together before God (cf. Confession, ch. 24, on marriage as a covenant of mutual help). It is not a verdict you get to issue by reading her conscience through the tenth commandment.

If she has been honest with you about wanting discretionary income and a few mornings out of the house, that's not a confession of covetousness. That's a wife telling you something about her life. Hear it as such.
