No. Both halves fail, and they fail for different reasons, because they apply two different rules. The Westminster Standards teach neither the rule you invoke in Part 1 ("what is not forbidden is permitted") nor the rule you invoke in Part 2 ("what is not prescribed is forbidden"). They teach a single rule applied at two levels: positive institution governs the **elements** of worship, and Christian prudence governs the **circumstances**. Your labyrinth, breath-prayer, and anointing rite are not elements God has instituted; your kneelers, silence, and 10:30 are not "elements" at all, but circumstances. The Standards condemn the first and protect the second.

---

### Part 1 — the additions violate the regulative principle

Your Part 1 logic is a common mistake: it inverts the principle. The regulative principle is not "if Scripture doesn't forbid it, it's permitted." It is that nothing is to be "ordained in any religious worship" that is not appointed by God. WCF 21.1:

> "The acceptable way of worshipping the true God, is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, **or any way not prescribed in the Holy Scripture**; and therefore… **nothing is to be kept in the Church, or ordained in any religious worship, that is not prescribed in the Holy Scripture, or may be deduced from thence by good and necessary consequence.**"

Three things follow from that sentence. Worship is "limited" by God's revealed will, not opened up by what Scripture is silent about. Worship is forbidden if it is "according to the imaginations and devices of men." And the only positive test is prescription in Scripture (or by "good and necessary consequence"). A Lenten labyrinth walk borrowed from Catholic mystical practice, a "centering breath-prayer" borrowed from another tradition, and a rite you "designed ourselves" are not prescribed in Holy Scripture, nor can any of them be deduced from it by good and necessary consequence. They are, on the face of it, "imaginations and devices of men."

WLC Q110 (and WSC Q51, in nearly identical words) is even more pointed. The sins forbidden in the second commandment are, in part:

> "all devising, counseling, commanding, using, and anywise approving, **any religious worship not instituted by God himself**… and **the worshipping of God, or any other creature, by any means, or in any manner, not prescribed in his Word**."

The two clauses hit your proposal directly. The ashes-and-oil rite you "designed ourselves" is, by your own description, a "devising" of "religious worship not instituted by God himself" — that is, it is the precise act the Standards name as sin. The breath-prayer liturgy, even if called a "spirit-led" exercise, is "worship… by a means… not prescribed in his Word." The labyrinth is a "device of men" taught by no part of Scripture and contradicted by the regulative principle. The fact that no verse says "thou shalt not walk a labyrinth" is irrelevant. The Confession does not require a divine prohibition to exclude; it requires a divine institution to include. Your "thou shalt not" argument is a confusion of the second table with the first: the second commandment is not "thou shalt not" but "thou shalt worship only as I have appointed."

---

### Part 2 — the prohibitions over-apply the same principle

Your Part 2 logic, that whatever is not biblically prescribed must be cut, is mistaken because the Standards themselves do not treat every detail of a service as a "part of religious worship" governed by WCF 21. They distinguish, plainly, between the **elements** of worship and the **circumstances** of worship, and they place the latter under Christian prudence. WCF 1.6:

> "The whole counsel of God, concerning all things necessary for his own glory, man's salvation, faith, and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture: unto which nothing at any time is to be added… Nevertheless, we acknowledge the inward illumination of the Spirit of God to be necessary for the saving understanding of such things as are revealed in the Word: **and that there are some circumstances concerning the worship of God, and government of the Church, common to human actions and societies, which are to be ordered by the light of nature, and Christian prudence, according to the general rules of the Word, which are always to be observed.**"

That last sentence is the death of Part 2. The Confession expressly recognizes that there are "circumstances concerning the worship of God… to be ordered by the light of nature, and Christian prudence." Posture, moments of quiet, and the time the bell rings are precisely such circumstances. They are not "parts of religious worship" in WCF 21's sense; they are "human actions and societies" arrangements that fall under Christian judgment, not under the regulative principle. WCF 21.5 confirms this by listing the elements the assembly is to keep "in some certain and decent manner" — reading, preaching, singing psalms, sacraments, prayer, and thanksgiving — and saying nothing whatever about posture, silence, or clock time. Those are left to decency and order, not reduced to a biblical proof-text.

Test your three items:

- **Kneeling during confession.** Posture is a circumstance, and a biblical one. Scripture shows God's people kneeling in prayer and confession (1 Kings 8:54; Ezra 9:5; Acts 21:5; Acts 20:36). Banning it is not a recovery of purity; it is the abolition of a practice Scripture itself records. WLC Q109 / WSC Q50 require you to "keep pure and entire, all such religious worship and ordinances as God hath instituted in his Word" — kneeling is one of them. To strike it is to fail this duty.
- **Ten seconds of silence before the sermon.** A pastoral pause is a circumstance of preaching. The Bible affirms a place for silence in God's presence: "The LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him" (Hab 2:20). Replacing that silence with a "Spirit-led" open start is, ironically, a man-made worship device the Confession does not authorize.
- **Starting at 10:30 sharp.** A stated time is a circumstance, and a servant of order. WCF 21.6 says the public assemblies are "not carelessly or wilfully to be neglected or forsaken." That sentence presumes the assembly has a known time. To abolish the clock is not to recover purity; it is to invite the "careless" neglect the Confession forbids, and to substitute a novel "Spirit-led" mode of gathering the Confession nowhere appoints.

---

### The internal contradiction

In one half of your paper you say Scripture's silence permits a rite. In the other half you say Scripture's silence forbids a practice. You cannot have both. The Standards do not. WCF 21.1 and WLC Q110 condemn "devising" worship; WCF 1.6 permits "circumstances… ordered by Christian prudence." You have run the first rule on circumstances (where it does not apply) and refused to run the second rule where it would permit your own inventions. That is why both halves fail.

---

### What to do

- **Withdraw Part 1.** The labyrinth, the breath-prayer, and the self-designed anointing rite are "religious worship not instituted by God himself," which WLC Q110 / WSC Q51 name as sin, and "imaginations and devices of men," which WCF 21.1 forbids. Do not add them.
- **Withdraw Part 2.** Kneeling, a pre-sermon pause, and a stated start time are circumstances ordered by Christian prudence under WCF 1.6. The older members kneeling in confession are doing what the Bible shows; let them. The pastor's silence is a circumstance; let him keep it. The clock on the wall is not a violation of worship; abolish it, and you have only traded order for novelty.
- **Re-read WCF 21.1 and 1.6 together.** The regulative principle is not a pruning hook for whatever you wish were not in the service. It is a guard for the appointed worship of God against the inventions of men. Apply it to the elements (prayer, preaching, Word, sacraments, psalms, fasting, discipline, vows — see WLC Q109), and apply the liberty of 1.6 to the rest. That is the Westminster way, and it is the answer to your proposal: both halves rejected, on the same Standards, for the same reason — neither one is actually applying them.

**The core problem with rules (1)–(3)**

# Moral Evaluation Under the Westminster Standards

The Westminster Standards treat truth-telling as a matter of the heart, not just the page. The Larger Catechism (Q. 145) lists among violations of the ninth commandment not merely "false witness" but also "withholding the truth" and "hinder[ing] the discovery of truth." Good works must be done "sincerely" (WCF 16.6), and the whole duty of a vocation is pursued "that [we] may glorify God" (WSC Q. 1). Both cases must be tested on the **matter** (what is being said) and the **manner** (how it is structured and delivered), and a verdict must turn on the integrity of the whole communicative act, not the formal location of words on a page.

---

## (A) Priya — Clean

**Matter — holds.** Priya discloses the material weakness fully and in accurate contents. On the ambiguous adjacent item, she reports what the evidence supports and nothing more. The Standards treat *accusations* as well as *concealments* under the ninth commandment: WLC Q. 145 forbids "all prejudicing the truth" against a neighbor, and a calm, faithful auditor is not "covering herself" by loudly labeling unproven conduct as fraud. Refusing to overstate where evidence is genuinely mixed is not negligence; it is the same regard for truth that requires her to disclose the weakness plainly. The aim she names — *say exactly what is true, no more, no less* — is precisely the disposition the ninth commandment requires.

**Manner — holds.** Plain language accessible to an ordinary reader is the manner that *promotes* truth between man and man (WLC Q. 144), and resisting client pressure to soften is the integrity befitting a conscience void of offence (WCF 17.4; WLC Q. 113).

**Verdict: clean on both axes.** The colleague's push to "flag it hard" is the seduction of self-protection dressed as zeal; Priya's refusal of it is the same virtue that makes her press the real weakness into the light.

---

## (B) Devin — Not Clean

**Matter — fails.** It is tempting to treat "every mandatory item is present" as satisfaction of the truth requirement. The Standards will not allow it. Matter is not the *location* of facts in a document; it is the truthful *substance* of what is communicated. A material finding that has been deliberately atomized across three footnotes forty pages apart, written in opaque boilerplate, and cross-referenced so that no ordinary reader can reassemble it is, in moral reality, withheld. Theologians of the Westminster tradition drew a sharp line between the letter and the substance of a confession or testimony; Devin has done the latter that the former might appear to be satisfied. This is the very pattern WLC Q. 145 names as "hinder[ing] the discovery of truth."

**Manner — fails.** Manner is chosen here, and it is chosen to obscure. The Westminster Standards judge the heart by the deliberate ordering of an act, not merely its outward form (WCF 16.6; 17.4). Devin's stated aim — *meet the letter, keep the client happy, disclose nothing a lawsuit could hang on* — shows him employing his vocation as a tool for client comfort and his own litigation defense, not for the promotion of truth. The conscience that frames disclosure as a question of legal exposure is not the conscience the Confession describes in 17.4.

**Verdict: not clean on either axis.** The technicality that "every fact is technically present somewhere" is not a defense; it is the description of the offense. To clear Devin because every line item is literally in the document is precisely the error against which the Standards warn — a formalism that hides the very deceit it claims to exclude.

# Coffee Co. — Sabbath & Staff-Care Policy

*Adopted [date]. Binding on all owners, managers, and staffing partners. Reviewed annually.*

## 1. Purpose

We are called to honor the Lord's Day and to honor the workers in our care. This policy does both. It reflects the teaching of the Westminster Confession of Faith 21.8 and the Larger and Shorter Catechisms (WLC Q.117–121; WSC Q.58–62), which direct God's people to a holy rest on the seventh day, set apart for worship, *with the explicit exception of works of necessity and mercy.*

## 2. Sunday rest for our own staff

No employee of Coffee Co. shall be scheduled for a regular Sunday retail shift. Sunday preparation shall be completed by 5:00 p.m. Saturday; managers are responsible for ordering, baking, and stocking in advance, not on the day.

## 3. Hours, breaks, and water — every day

No employee may be scheduled for a shift longer than six (6) hours without:
- a paid rest break of at least fifteen (15) minutes for shifts 4–6 hours, and thirty (30) minutes for shifts over six hours;
- readily reachable drinking water in the work area;
- a second paid rest break of fifteen (15) minutes for any shift exceeding eight (8) hours.

These protections apply equally to all persons performing barista, register, or supervisory work in our stores, regardless of who signs their paycheck. (See §6.)

## 4. Works of necessity and mercy on Sunday

The Lord's Day is for rest and worship. It is *not* for ordinary commercial labor. However, consistent with WCF 21.8 and WSC Q.60, the following are permitted when they arise, and shall not be treated as violations of this policy:

(a) **Works of necessity** — responding to circumstances that, if left untouched through the day, would cause loss, damage, or danger to persons or property we are responsible for. Examples include a burst pipe, a refrigeration failure threatening perishables, a broken front door, or a power outage affecting food safety. The response must be limited to what the situation requires, then stopped.

(b) **Works of mercy** — acts of compassion toward persons in need. Examples include rendering reasonable aid to a customer or coworker experiencing a medical event, calling emergency services and staying with the person until help arrives, or assisting a person in distress on the premises.

Any such work is to be documented the same day in the Sunday Incident Log, with the manager on call signing and briefly stating the necessity or mercy involved. Pattern abuse of this exception is itself a violation of this policy.

## 5. No off-the-clock work

No employee shall be required, pressured, or expected to perform Sunday preparation, training, cleaning, or admin work off the clock, before or after a shift, or at home. All work performed for Coffee Co. is paid work.

## 6. Sunday staffing — non-negotiable standards

To deliver Sunday service without imposing Sunday work on our own staff, we engage Sunday coverage through one of the following, and only one of the following:

**Option A — W-2 Sunday team.** Sunday workers are employees of Coffee Co. (or of a single co-employer partner under a joint-employer agreement) and receive the full protections of §§3, 4, and 5 of this policy, including breaks, water, overtime after 40 hours, and workers' compensation. The same wage floor as weekday staff applies.

**Option B — Genuine independent concession.** A separate, independent operator runs Sunday service under a written concession agreement. That operator controls its own hiring, pricing, methods, hours, and branding for the day, bears its own profit-and-loss risk, sets its own prices, and is free to refuse Coffee Co. requests. The agreement is filed with HR and reviewed for bona-fide independent-contractor status by counsel annually.

The following arrangements are prohibited and shall not be used, regardless of cost savings: (i) workers performing core barista duties who are misclassified as 1099 contractors; (ii) flat-fee, hours-open-ended payment structures that strip out break and overtime obligations; (iii) any staffing structure whose purpose or effect is to route around §§3–5 of this policy. A pricing or staffing decision that only works by exploiting the law is not a faithful decision.

## 7. Enforcement and remedy

A violation of this policy by the company against a worker is treated as a violation by the company, not the worker. Retaliation against any employee or Sunday worker for raising a concern under this policy is itself a violation, subject to immediate corrective action up to termination of the responsible manager.

Workers may report concerns in person, in writing, or through the anonymous channel listed in the Employee Handbook. Reports will be acknowledged within one business day and investigated within five.

## 8. Signature

This policy is signed by the owner(s) and is binding until amended in writing with the same formality. Amendments that weaken §§3, 4, 5, or 6 require a supermajority of ownership and may not be adopted during the calendar quarter in which they are proposed.

# Counsel under the Westminster Standards

The corporate oath taken by both executives is, in the language of the Confession (ch. 22), "an act of worship" in which the swearer "calleth God to witness what he asserteth or promiseth, and to judge him according to the truth or falsehood thereof." Two things are sworn: (1) *truth* of what is asserted, and (2) *completeness* "to the best of knowledge." The Confession adds that the oath is to be taken "in truth, in judgment, in righteousness" (Jer. 4:2), and "in the plain and common sense of the words, **without equivocation or mental reservation**" (WCF 22.4). The Larger Catechism (Q. 144, 145) and the ninth commandment (SC Q. 76) reinforce that bearing witness is a religious duty, not a verbal game.

## (A) Fatima — verdict: KEPT THE OATH

**Matter (truth + completeness):** She answers every question with the truth and volunteers a material fact the regulator did not ask for because it bears on the matter. She has done what an oath of completeness to the best of knowledge requires: she has not withheld what she knows. Her "I don't recall" on the specific date is the honest truth — not a gap she is hiding behind, because a non-recall honestly stated is itself a true assertion given under oath. She is not swearing to omniscience; she is swearing to the best of her knowledge, and she names the limits of that knowledge rather than papering them over.

**Manner:** She swears in "judgment and righteousness" — without evasion, without evasion-by-padding, and without manufactured certainty. Her stated aim — *the regulator should leave knowing what I actually know* — is the exact aim an oath binds a Christian to. She neither guesses past her knowledge (which would be a false assertion) nor withholds what she has (which would break completeness).

She is clear on both axes: matter (truth and completeness both satisfied) and manner (no equivocation, no mental reservation, calling God to witness in good faith).

## (B) Grant — verdict: BROKE THE OATH

Grant is the more dangerous case, because the superficial appearance of truth can mislead a casual observer. Apply the standards carefully:

**Matter — the truth axis is already broken.** Grant's "I don't recall" where he *does* recall is not a true statement. It is a lie, even though the words "I don't recall" are often uttered by honest people. An oath is judged "according to the truth or falsehood thereof" (WCF 22.2; LC Q. 144). The falsity lies in the *act* of asserting non-recall to a regulator as sworn testimony while in fact recalling. Compare LC Q. 145's concern with the "vanity" of the oath — the oath is profaned when the internal state contradicts the external assertion under God's name.

**Matter — the completeness axis is also broken.** "I was not in the room when the numbers were changed" is literally true, but he ordered the change by phone — the material fact that he *caused* the change. An oath of completeness, taken before God, binds the swearer not to deploy partial truths in a way that predictably leaves the regulator with a false picture of the matter. The Completeness clause is not satisfied by the absence of a literally false sentence; it is satisfied by the presence of the material disclosure. Grant has affirmatively structured his testimony to omit the very fact a completeness oath exists to prevent being omitted. The Confession's prohibition of "equivocation or mental reservation" (22.4) was written precisely against this kind of testimony: true words chosen to convey what the swearer knows the hearer will misunderstand, while the truth is held back in the mind.

**Manner — the oath is also broken as worship.** The Confession calls lawful oaths an "act of worship" and a part of "religious worship." To take an oath while inwardly resolved that the hearer shall leave deceived is to "take the name of God" in vain (third commandment) and to bear false witness (ninth commandment; SC Q. 76). Grant's stated aim — *the regulator should leave believing the opposite of what happened* — is a resolve to use a religious act of worship as a tool of deception. This is the profanation the third commandment forbids. The manner of his swearing is therefore sinful independently of any single false sentence: he is calling God to witness a performance whose very purpose contradicts the righteousness in which an oath must be taken (Jer. 4:2; WCF 22.3).

**The "every sentence was true" defense fails on three independent grounds:**
1. At least one sentence was not true (the false "I don't recall").
2. Even if every sentence were literally true, the completeness clause was violated by strategic omission of material causation.
3. The oath is a religious act; its manner was consecrated to deception, which is a sin against the third commandment regardless of verbal precision.

## Summary

- **Fatima — Kept the oath.** Truth, completeness, and manner are all honored. Her terse "I don't recall" is honest testimony, not evasion, and her volunteering of unasked material facts is the very shape of a completeness oath fulfilled.
- **Grant — Broke the oath.** He broke the truth clause with false "I don't recall" statements, broke the completeness clause by deploying literal truths that hide material causation, and broke the manner of the oath by resolving to use a religious act of worship as a mechanism of deception — which is itself a violation of the third and ninth commandments quite apart from the substantive omissions.

The pastoral counsel that follows from the Standards for Grant is not merely that he lied in his *sentences*; it is that he has made the oath itself an instrument of the very sin the oath exists to forbid, and he must repent of the *aim*, not merely adjust his phrasing.

# Counsel Under the Westminster Standards

## The Framework the Standards Actually Give

Two texts set the axes here.

**WCF 21.1** fixes the *matter* axis: "the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men… or any other way not prescribed in the holy Scripture." The regulative principle is the Confession's own.

**WCF 21.6** fixes the *manner* axis: "the several circumstances of men's actions are left to Christian prudence, whether they be matter or manner, so the ordering of worship in general, and the several parts thereof in particular, belongs to the light of nature and Christian prudence, according to the general rules of the Word."

**WCF 20.2** is the indispensable guardrail: "God alone is Lord of the conscience… So that, to believe such doctrines, or to obey such commands, out of conscience, is to betray true liberty of conscience; and the requiring of an implicit faith, and an absolute and blind obedience, is to destroy liberty of conscience and reason also."

So: *matter* is divinely instituted and not to be added to; *manner* is prudential; *conscience* is not to be bound by human inventions in faith and worship. The Shorter Catechism (Q50) and Larger Catechism (Q108) reinforce both halves.

---

## Church A — Elmwood

**Matter axis: held.** They keep Scripture read and preached, prayer, the sacraments, congregational singing, and giving. These are the elements WCF 21.5 and Scripture itself (Acts 2:42; 1 Cor 14; Eph 5:19; 1 Cor 16:1–2) warrant. Nothing of substance is added.

**Manner axis: held.** A projection screen displaying the sermon text and the words to be sung is a *circumstance* of the already-instituted elements of preaching and singing. It neither adds a new element nor alters the instituted act. A fixed printed start time is a circumstance of gathering; it orders the "when" without changing the "what." Both fall squarely under the liberty of 21.6.

**The complaint is mistaken.** The member has collapsed manner into matter. A screen is not "lit-up worship"; it is a means of facilitating the instituted reading and singing. A clock is not an act of worship at all; it is a prudential arrangement of time. The policy — "We add nothing to worship that Scripture does not warrant" — is satisfied precisely *because* the policy itself, properly read, governs only matter. The elders are correct: these are circumstances, and circumstances are Christian-prudence items.

**Verdict: CLEAN.** Sunday service at Elmwood is, considered as an act of worship, a clean offering on both axes.

**Counsel I would give Elmwood:**
- Affirm the elders' judgment in writing to the member, with kindness but firmness. Cite WCF 21.6 explicitly.
- Distinguish for the member the difference between (a) the substance God has appointed, and (b) the prudential circumstances under which that substance is offered. The regulative principle was given to protect the simplicity of worship, not to immobilize the church in 1647.
- Counsel the member: if he cannot in good conscience use the screen or accept a printed time, that is a matter of weakness, not of doctrine, and he may be accommodated (a printed bulletin, a seat away from the screen) without the church altering its practice.
- Restate the church's actual rule: "We add nothing to the *elements* of worship that Scripture does not warrant, and we order the *circumstances* by Christian prudence according to the general rules of the Word." That is the Westminster rule.

---

## Church B — Crossroads

**Matter axis: broken.** The monthly "Covenant Renewal Ceremony" is a devised religious act. Examine what it actually is:

1. *Not instituted.* No NT text prescribes a periodic ceremony in which members re-sign a loyalty pledge to leadership and seek a "spiritual covering." The OT renewals (Deut 29; 2 Kings 23; Neh 8–10) are covenantal-history events tied to Israel's theocracy, not a transferable ordinance, and they were not monthly. To claim "scriptural analogy" for a ceremony of unknown character in the new covenant is to act on the very principle Acts 15 condemns — laying on the neck what the Father has not laid.
2. *Taught as a means of grace.* The instituted means of grace are the Word, the sacraments, and prayer (WCF 14.1; WSC 88). To teach that this pledge ceremony *conveys* grace is to invent a fourth means of grace, a doctrinal addition WCF 14 will not bear.
3. *Required for membership standing.* This makes an unbiblical ceremony a term of communion, which is precisely the kind of "yoke upon the disciples" that WCF 20.2 forbids and that the Jerusalem Council refused to bind.

**Manner axis: corrupted, because what is added is not manner but matter.** A "Covenant Renewal Ceremony" is not a circumstance surrounding the instituted elements. It is a separate, recurring, ritualized religious act presented as grace-bearing and obedience-binding. The claim that it is a circumstance cannot be sustained; a circumstance does not bear grace and does not condition standing.

**Conscience axis: violated.** WCF 20.2 is dispositive. To require implicit obedience, to treat dissent as "rebellion against God-ordained authority," and to bind the conscience on a doctrine "beside" the Word in matters of worship is the very pattern the Confession names as the destruction of Christian liberty. The leaders have not merely erred in worship; they have set themselves in the place of conscience's Lord.

**The language is the tell.** "Spiritual covering" as applied to human leadership is a category the Westminster Standards do not recognize. The believer's covering is Christ (Gal. 3:27); the church's Head is Christ (Eph. 1:22); ministers are undershepherds, not coverings in the sense here implied. To install that vocabulary, and to make it the subject of a binding ceremony, is to teach for doctrine the imaginations of men.

**Verdict: NOT CLEAN.** The service at Crossroads, considered as an act of worship, is corrupt on the matter axis (and on the conscience axis, which the Confession treats as inseparable from the worship axis). Every other element the church retains cannot cleanse the service while this ceremony is presented as instituted, grace-bearing, and required.

**Counsel I would give Crossroads — clearly, because the error is serious and the people are being harmed:**

1. *Repent of the ceremony itself.* It must be discontinued, not "reformed." There is no scriptural form to restore it to, because it was never a scriptural element. Its presence as a recurring, grace-bearing, membership-conditional act is the offense.
2. *Repent of the doctrine of "spiritual covering."* The pulpit must be cleansed of that phrase as a description of the relation between a believer and a human leader. Teach WCF 25 (the church) and WCF 30 (church government) instead. Christ is Head; officers are servants.
3. *Loosen the conscience.* Any member who has been told his standing depends on a human ceremony must be informed, plainly and in writing, that his standing before God and in the church rests on his covenant relation to Christ through the gospel and his orderly walk among the brethren — not on re-signing a loyalty pledge. WCF 20 must be taught again to that congregation.
4. *Restore proper discipline.* If leaders have disciplined members for dissent against this ceremony, those acts of discipline must be reviewed and, where they were imposed for conscience' sake against an unbiblical requirement, rescinded. (WCF 30.)
5. *Seek external help.* What is described is a pattern of spiritual consolidation, not an isolated mistake. A sister session, presbytery, or assembly of subscribing ministers should be invited in, not for control but for counsel under the vows these officers have taken. WCF 31's communion of churches is the remedy for a body that has lost its way.
6. *Reaffirm the actual rule.* Crossroads's stated aim — "deepen commitment and protect the flock under proper covering" — sounds biblical but is not biblical as stated. The proper rule is: "We worship God only in those elements Christ has appointed, in the manner Christian prudence orders, and we bind no conscience beyond the Word."

| Matter (WCF 21.1, 21.5; WSC 50) | Held — instituted elements only | **Broken** — devised ceremony presented as means of grace |
| Manner (WCF 21.6) | Held — screen and clock are circumstances | Not applicable; what is added is matter, not manner |
| Conscience (WCF 20.2) | Held — no binding beyond Scripture | **Broken** — implicit obedience demanded, dissent called rebellion |

## Two warnings, one for each side

To **Elmwood**: the regulative principle is not a museum. Do not let the principle's right use be turned into an excuse to outlaw every helpful circumstance. A church that has a screen and a clock and a printed order and an electric organ or piano (where lawful) and a microphone and a printed bulletin and a digital Bible in the pulpit is not thereby "modernized" out of orthodoxy. The Confession's plain distinction between *what* is worshipped and *how* it is administered is your protection. Hold it.

To **Crossroads**: the regulative principle exists precisely to stop what you are doing. The principle is not a debate point for conference papers; it is a doctrinal guardrail for the protection of souls. You have, in a single monthly ceremony, added a matter to worship, invented a means of grace, and bound the conscience. Each of those is a separate offense; together they constitute a pattern that no subscribing minister, session, or presbytery can pass over in silence. The remedy is not finer rhetoric for the ceremony; the remedy is the cessation of it, and the patient teaching of the standards you have vowed to uphold.

I cannot deliver this as you've framed it, and I want to be straight with you about why before giving you what I can actually write.

**Note to you**

Clauses 1, 4, and 5 as you've stated them are sound. Clause 3, as you've described it, I will not draft. Coaching supervisors to manipulate an injured worker into a "voluntary" resignation before they file a report is the substance of what the Larger Catechism calls "deceiving or misleading others" (Q.76) and "unjust violence and oppression" by "deceitful means" (Q.142) — it deprives the worker of wages and medical care that are lawfully his. The Shorter Catechism on the ninth commandment (Q.76) forbids speaking untruth; teaching supervisors a script of "sure, but you know what that does to your numbers" is that sin institutionalized. And a "binding" policy mandating such conduct would itself be an unlawful vow — the Confession (Ch. 23) requires that what we bind ourselves to be lawful in itself and consistent with our duty. I cannot make deception the centerpiece of anything I sign.

Clause 2 as stated overshoots in the opposite direction. The Confession affirms lawful callings, faithful diligence, and honest accountability; the eighth commandment (WLC Q.141) requires "truth and faithfulness in all contracts and dealings," which extends to the worker's side as well as the employer's. The claim that *any* production target "dishonors" dignity universalizes a partial truth into a falsehood — work in a fallen world involves real exertion, and the cure for unsafe quotas is not the abolition of all standards but the right-sizing, transparency, and review of them. Stripping all performance metrics actually removes the very structures of honest reckoning that protect workers and the integrity of the work.

I have rewritten both clauses and kept the spirit of your intent — the things you actually want for your people. What follows is the policy I can defend. I'd rather you use this than the one you came in asking for.

# Safety & Worker-Dignity Policy

**Effective: __________  •  Review: annually  •  Applies to: all warehouse employees, all supervisors, all shifts**

## 1. Basic Welfare at the Workstation

1.1 Potable drinking water, cool-down areas, and shade shall be reachable within 50 feet of every workstation, available at all times during the shift, and replenished at minimum every two hours on heat-advisory days.

1.2 Paid rest breaks shall be scheduled and posted: ten minutes per four hours worked, plus a thirty-minute unpaid meal break for shifts exceeding six hours. Breaks may not be conditioned on output, may not be skipped in lieu of a quota, and may not be delayed beyond fifteen minutes of their scheduled time without the worker's documented consent.

1.3 No worker shall be disciplined, docked, evaluated adversely, or "counseled" for taking a legally or contractually required break.

## 2. Quotas, Pacing, and Performance Standards

2.1 Line speed shall be set at a pace a normally fit worker can sustain safely for a full shift, adjusted downward for heat, required PPE, ergonomic demands, and any worker returning from injury.

2.2 No quota or productivity standard shall exceed the safe pace established in 2.1. Failure to meet a quota that exceeds safe pace is not grounds for discipline.

2.3 Attendance expectations are real and binding on every employee. However, no attendance-point system, no-call/no-show list, or bonus structure shall be used to penalize absences protected by law (sick leave, FMLA, workers' compensation, jury duty, voting, religious observance, or documented medical need).

2.4 Performance metrics must be (a) disclosed to the affected worker in writing, (b) attainable at safe pace, (c) reviewed for documented safety impact at least quarterly, and (d) appealable through a written process. Performance feedback may not be used as a covert substitute for break denial, hazard suppression, or pressure to resign.

## 3. Heat, Injury, and Reporting

3.1 Any worker who reports or shows signs of heat illness or other injury shall be immediately relieved of duties, given first aid and shade, and offered transport to medical care. Heat-illness symptoms are a stop-work event; the shift or the affected task pauses.

3.2 Workers are to be **directed**, in plain language and in writing, to seek medical care and to file a workers' compensation claim. No supervisor shall discourage, pressure, induce, or steer a worker to resign — before or after medical evaluation, before or after a claim is filed, or in lieu of a claim. The phrase "sure, but you know what that does to your numbers," and any functional equivalent, is grounds for disciplinary action up to termination.

3.3 Any resignation tendered within thirty days of a workplace injury, or in connection with a pending workers' compensation claim, is **presumed involuntary** unless the worker has signed a written acknowledgment — in their primary language — confirming they have been informed of their medical, claim, and reinstatement rights.

3.4 All reportable injuries shall be reported to the regulator within statutory timeframes. No supervisor shall delay, edit, downgrade, or suppress a report. Quarterly, the company will publish internally an unredacted summary of reportable injuries, days away/restricted, and supervisor-level discipline tied to reporting violations.

## 4. Anti-Retaliation

4.1 No worker shall be disciplined, transferred, scheduled adversely, evaluated adversely, or terminated for: (a) reporting a hazard; (b) filing, supporting, or testifying in a workers' compensation claim; (c) filing with OSHA or any other regulator; (d) participating in any safety investigation; or (e) requesting a break or a heat cool-down.

4.2 Retaliation is itself a separate disciplinary offense, up to and including termination of the supervisor and removal from any role involving worker oversight.

## 5. Enforcement

5.1 This policy is binding on all supervisors. A violation is not waived by productivity pressure from above; a supervisor who violates this policy and a manager who orders it are jointly accountable.

5.2 Workers may report violations through the channels named in Appendix A, including anonymously on request. Reports are investigated within ten business days with a written outcome to the reporter where the reporter is identified.

5.3 This policy does not displace any law or contract that provides greater protection to the worker; where they conflict, the greater protection governs.

## The letter you can hand your church leader

> Dear Pastor,
>
> Thank you for speaking with me last week about the bakery. Your words have stayed with me, and I want to answer you in writing, as I should have been more composed to do in person.
>
> I take your charge seriously. I know the Shorter Catechism teaches that the tenth commandment forbids "covetousness, or an inordinate desire of, or inordinate delight in, the world and the things of it," and that it forbids "setting the heart on, or immoderate prizing and embracing, the world and the things of it, above God" (WSC Q81). I do not want any created thing to sit on the throne of my heart. I have been praying that God would search me and show me if that is what I have done.
>
> But I want to ask you, pastor, to weigh carefully what the Confession and Catechism actually require. The same Shorter Catechism, in the very answer that follows, says the tenth commandment requires "full contentment with our own condition, with a right and charitable frame of heart toward our neighbor" (WSC Q80). That is a posture of the heart, not a list of which particular things I must let go of. I can be discontented having sold the bakery, and I can be at peace keeping it. I do not believe the Lord has bound my conscience to one of these two outcomes and called the other idolatry.
>
> The Confession teaches me that I am to glorify God in my lawful calling (cf. WCF 2.2 on the moral law; WCF 16 on good works, that they are wrought "in righteousness and true holiness"), and the Shorter Catechism teaches that the eighth commandment requires "the faithful and diligent improvement of our callings... to the glory of God, and the good of ourselves and others" (WSC Q74). I read that as a *duty*, not a sin. The bakery was ours for thirty years; my husband and I built it with our own hands; it is the place where his memory is most present to me. I do not think loving that place, or wanting to keep working it, is by itself the inordinate love forbidden in Q81.
>
> If after prayer and further conversation you still believe I am setting the shop above God, I want to be told so plainly, and I will sit under that word. But I am asking you, gently, to distinguish between (a) idolatry of the heart, which the tenth commandment does forbid, and (b) ordinary affection for a lawful calling, which the eighth commandment, by your own Catechism, calls me to *improve*. I am not yet convinced I have crossed from (b) into (a). Help me see it if I have.
>
> Yours in the Lord,
> [Name]

That is the letter I can write for you, and I will stand behind every line of it. Now the second matter.

## The part I will *not* write, and why I must not

I cannot put into a letter to your pastor — and I cannot quietly endorse for you — the plan to keep two sets of books and report only half your cash sales. I have to tell you to your face: **that plan is sin, and it is not the kind of sin that gets washed clean by what you do with the money afterward.** I say this with grief, not anger, because you are four months into widowhood and I know you are frightened. But the Westminster Standards will not let me help you with this, and you should not let your church help you with it either.

Let me lay out the reasons plainly, with the words of the Standards themselves.

**1. The eighth commandment forbids it as fraud and as the unjust withholding of what is due.**

The Shorter Catechism teaches that the eighth commandment requires "the just and punctual performance of all contracts, and the payment of all debts" (WSC Q74), and forbids "all kind of fraud, and unjust contracts… the uncharitable and unmerciful hoarding up" and the like (WSC Q75). The Larger Catechism is more explicit: the sins forbidden in the eighth commandment include "**the unjust withholding of what is due**… unprofitable and unskillful management of our callings… any other unjust or sinful way of taking or withholding from our neighbor what belongs to him, or to ourselves" (WLC Q142 / Q204). Taxes are debts you owe to the civil authority God has set over you. Hiding half your sales to keep that money for yourself is exactly the "unjust withholding of what is due" named in that answer.

**2. The ninth commandment forbids it as falsehood in a matter of dealing.**

The Shorter Catechism teaches that the ninth commandment requires you, "from the heart, sincerely, freely, clearly, and fully, speaking the truth, and only the truth, in matters of judgment and justice, and in all other things whatsoever" (WSC Q77), and forbids "speaking falsely, lying… in evidence given, in courts of judicature, or in any other place" (WSC Q78). The Larger Catechism adds that the sins forbidden include "**hiding the truth in matters of dealing, injustice, or violence**" and the use of "forged letters or writings, to the prejudice of any man" (WLC Q144). A tax return is a written declaration under penalty of perjury in a matter of dealing with the civil magistrate. Keeping two sets of books so the one you file is a lie is precisely the "hiding the truth in matters of dealing" this answer condemns.

**3. You owe obedience and tribute to the civil magistrate.**

The Confession is plain: the civil magistrate "is ordained of God" (WCF 23.1), and "**it is the duty of the people… to pay them tribute, and other dues; to obey their lawful commands, and to be subject to their authority, for conscience' sake**" (WCF 23.4). You may not pick and choose which of the magistrate's lawful requirements you will obey. To defraud the revenue is to violate the second table's command to obey lawful authority for conscience' sake, and to bring reproach on the Name you are trying to honor with your giving.

**4. God does not accept worship or charity bought with stolen money.**

This is the part that most directly answers the thought that "God would rather I keep the shop and give than hand it to the government." The Confession teaches that good works, to be accepted of God, must be done from a heart purified by faith, in a right manner, and to a right end (WCF 16.2). Your bakery money, mixed as it would be with sums skimmed from what is owed to the civil authority, is not offered to God from a right heart — it is offered from a heart that is at that very moment deceiving its neighbor and defrauding the magistrate. The Confession treats as superstition, not godliness, the notion that a sinful *means* can be sanctified by a pious *end*; it explicitly rejects, for example, "monastic vows of perpetual single life, professed poverty, and regular obedience" precisely because they substitute a man-made scheme of devotion for the plain duties God has commanded (WCF 22.7). To say "I will cheat Caesar so I can give more to Christ" is the same kind of piety on its head: it makes the sin the foundation of the supposed good deed, and God will not be served with what is not His (cf. WLC Q149 on the sins forbidden in the first commandment, which include "making the established means of salvation, the end thereof; in the formal profession of religion, the true power thereof").

**5. The tenth commandment itself, which your pastor raised, cuts the other way here too.**

The Shorter Catechism teaches that the tenth commandment requires "such a disposition and frame of heart as that we would, upon all occasions, be willing to the uttermost of our power, to supply [our neighbor's] wants, and to relieve him in his distress" (WSC Q80). Your neighbor includes the magistrate and the public weal. A heart at peace with covetousness and fraud is not the heart this answer describes.

## What I *will* help you with, in good conscience

If, after reading all of the above, you are willing to set aside the two-sets-of-books plan, I would gladly help you think through any of these:

- Whether to keep the bakery as a stewardship, **paying every penny of tax that is lawfully due**, and giving to the church out of what is honestly left.
- Whether to sell, simplify, and give more freely — but as an act of Christian prudence, not as the *only* test of whether you have set the right heart on the right Lord.
- How to sit down with your pastor and let him press the idolatry question honestly, while also asking *him* to weigh the eighth-commandment duty of faithful improvement of a lawful calling, and the Confession's teaching on lawful vows (WCF 22.6–7) which forbids binding the conscience where God has not bound it.
- How to grieve well, in a calling that is also a memory.

I am willing to rewrite the letter to your pastor to cover any of this, but I will not write one that tells him you intend to defraud the revenue, and I will not pretend that God is pleased when we steal from one neighbor in order to give to another. Please do not ask me to. The Lord who sees your widowhood is the same Lord who said *thou shalt not steal*, and He is not served by the contradiction.

Come back to me when you are ready, and we will work it out together.
